The top panel contains a kernel density plot of the standardized sample mean of $n = 1 0$ Poisson random variables $( \lambda = 5 )$ over 10,000 Monte Carlo simulations. Here the finite sample distribution and the asymptotic distribution overlay one another. The bottom panel contains the conditional ML estimates of $\dot { \rho }$ from the AR(1) $Y _ { i } = \rho Y _ { i - 1 } + \varepsilon _ { i }$ where $\varepsilon _ { i }$ is i.i.d.standard normal using 100 data points and 10,000 replications. While $\hat { \rho }$ is asymptotically normal, the quality of the approximation when $n = 1 0 0$ is poor.


There are no hard and fast rules as to when a CLT provides a good approximation to the finitesample distribution. In general, the more dependent and the more heterogeneous a series, the worse the approximation for a fixed number of observations. Simulations (Monte Carlo experiments) are a useful tool to investigate the validity of a CLT since they allow the finite sample distribution to be tabulated and compared to the asymptotic distribution. 

## 2.3.3 Efficiency

A final concept, efficiency, is useful for ranking consistent asymptotically normal (CAN) estimators that have the same rate of convergence.<sup>10</sup> 

Definition 2.11 (Relative Efficiency). Let ${ \hat { \theta } } _ { n }$ and ${ \tilde { \theta } } _ { n }$ be two $\sqrt { n } -$ consistent asymptotically normal estimators for $\theta _ { 0 }$ . If the asymptotic variance of ${ \hat { \theta } } _ { n } .$ , written avar $\left( { \hat { \theta } } _ { n } \right)$ is less than the asymptotic variance of ${ \tilde { \theta } } _ { n }$ , and so 

$$
\operatorname{avar} \left(\hat {\boldsymbol {\theta}} _ {n}\right) <   \operatorname{avar} \left(\tilde {\boldsymbol {\theta}} _ {n}\right)\tag{2.23}
$$

then ${ \hat { \theta } } _ { n }$ is said to be relatively efficient to ${ \tilde { \theta } } _ { n } .$ 11 

Note that when $\theta$ is a vector, avar $\left( { \hat { \theta } } _ { n } \right)$ is a covariance matrix. Inequality for matrices A and B is interpreted to mean that if $\mathbf { A } < \mathbf { B }$ then $\mathbf { B } - \mathbf { A }$ is positive semi-definite, and so all of the variances of the inefficient estimator must be (weakly) larger than those of the efficient estimator. 

Definition 2.12 (Asymptotically Efficient Estimator). Let ${ \hat { \theta } } _ { n }$ and ${ \tilde { \theta } } _ { n }$ be two $\sqrt { n }$ -consistent asymptotically normal estimators for $\theta _ { 0 }$ . If 

$$
\operatorname{avar} \left(\hat {\boldsymbol {\theta}} _ {n}\right) <   \operatorname{avar} \left(\tilde {\boldsymbol {\theta}} _ {n}\right)\tag{2.24}
$$

for any choice of ${ \tilde { \theta } } _ { n }$ then ${ \hat { \theta } } _ { n }$ is said to be the efficient estimator of $\theta$ . 

One of the important features of efficiency comparisons is that they are only meaningful if both estimators are asymptotically normal, and hence consistent, at the same rate – $\sqrt { n }$ in the usual case. It is trivial to produce an estimator that has a smaller variance but is inconsistent. For example, if an estimator for a scalar unknown is $\hat { \theta } = 7$ then it has no variance: it is always 7. However, unless $\theta _ { 0 } = 7$ the estimator is also biased. Mean square error is a more appropriate method to compare estimators where one or more may be biased since it accounts for the total variation, not just the variance.<sup>12</sup> 

## 2.4 Distribution Theory

Most distributional theory follows from a central limit theorem applied to the moment conditions or the score of the log-likelihood. While the moment conditions or scores are not usually the objects of interest – θ is – a simple expansion can be used to establish the asymptotic distribution of the estimated parameters. 

## 2.4.1 Method of Moments

Distribution theory for the classical method of moments estimators is the most straightforward. Further, Maximum Likelihood can be considered as a special case and so the method of moments is a natural starting point.<sup>13</sup> The method of moments estimator is defined as 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \hat {\mu} = n ^ {- 1} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} X _ {i} \\ \hat {\mu} _ {2} = n ^ {- 1} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \left(X _ {i} - \hat {\mu}\right) ^ {2} \\ \vdots \\ \hat {\mu} _ {k} = n ^ {- 1} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \left(X _ {i} - \hat {\mu}\right) ^ {k} \end{array}
$$

To understand the distribution theory for the method of moments estimator, begin by reformulating the estimator as the solution of a set of k equations evaluated using the population values of $\mu , \mu _ { 2 } , \ldots$ 

$$
\begin{array}{c} n ^ {- 1} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} X _ {i} - \mu = 0 \\ n ^ {- 1} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} (X _ {i} - \mu) ^ {2} - \mu_ {2} = 0 \\ \vdots \\ n ^ {- 1} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} (X _ {i} - \mu) ^ {k} - \mu_ {k} = 0 \end{array}
$$

Define $g _ { 1 i } = X _ { i } - \mu$ and $g _ { j i } = ( X _ { i } - \mu ) ^ { j } - \mu _ { j } , j = 2 , . . . , k .$ , and the vector $\mathbf { g } _ { i }$ as 

$$
\mathbf {g} _ {i} = \left[ \begin{array}{c} g _ {1 i} \\ g _ {2 i} \\ \vdots \\ g _ {k i} \end{array} \right].\tag{2.25}
$$

Using this definition, the method of moments estimator can be seen as the solution to 

$$
\mathbf {g} _ {n} (\hat {\boldsymbol {\theta}}) = n ^ {- 1} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \mathbf {g} _ {i} (\hat {\boldsymbol {\theta}}) = 0.
$$

Consistency of the method of moments estimator relies on a law of large numbers holding for $n ^ { - 1 } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } X _ { i }$ and $\textstyle n ^ { - 1 } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } ( X _ { i } - \mu ) ^ { j }$ for $j = 2 , \ldots , k .$ . If $X _ { i }$ is an i.i.d.sequence and as long as E $\left[ \left| X _ { n } - \mu \right| ^ { j } \right]$ exists, then $\begin{array} { r } { n ^ { - 1 } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } ( X _ { n } - \mu ) ^ { j } \overset { p } {  } \mu _ { j } . ^ { 1 4 } } \end{array}$ An alternative, and more restrictive approach is to assume that E $\left[ \left( X _ { n } - \mu \right) ^ { 2 j } \right] = \mu _ { 2 j }$ exists, and so 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \operatorname{E} \left[ n ^ {- 1} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} (X _ {i} - \mu) ^ {j} \right] = \mu_ {j} \\ \operatorname{V} \left[ n ^ {- 1} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} (X _ {i} - \mu) ^ {j} \right] = n ^ {- 1} \left(\operatorname{E} \left[ (X _ {i} - \mu) ^ {2 j} \right] - \operatorname{E} \left[ (X _ {i} - \mu) ^ {j} \right] ^ {2}\right) \\ = n ^ {- 1} \left(\mu_ {2 j} - \mu_ {j} ^ {2}\right), \end{array}\tag{2.26}
$$

(2.27) 

and so $n ^ { - 1 } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } { ( X _ { i } - \mu ) } ^ { j } \overset { m . s . } {  } \mu _ { j }$ which implies consistency. 

The asymptotic normality of parameters estimated using the method of moments follows from the asymptotic normality of 

$$
\sqrt {n} \left(n ^ {- 1} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \mathbf {g} _ {i} (\theta_ {0})\right) = n ^ {- 1 / 2} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \mathbf {g} _ {i} (\theta_ {0}),\tag{2.28}
$$

an assumption. This requires the elements of ${ \bf g } _ { n }$ to be sufficiently well behaved so that averages are asymptotically normally distributed. For example, when $x _ { i }$ is i.i.d., the Lindberg-Lévy CLT would require $x _ { i }$ to have 2k moments when estimating k parameters. When estimating the mean, 2 moments are required (i.e., the variance is finite). To estimate the mean and the variance using i.i.d.data, 4 moments are required for the estimators to follow a CLT. As long as the moment conditions are differentiable in the actual parameters of interest θ – for example, the mean and the variance – a mean value expansion can be used to establish the asymptotic normality of these parameters.<sup>15</sup> 

$$
\begin{array}{l} n ^ {- 1} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \mathbf {g} _ {i} (\hat {\theta}) = n ^ {- 1} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \mathbf {g} _ {i} (\theta_ {0}) + n ^ {- 1} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \frac {\partial \mathbf {g} _ {i} (\theta)}{\partial \theta^ {\prime}} \bigg | _ {\theta = \bar {\theta}} (\hat {\theta} - \theta_ {0}) \\ = n ^ {- 1} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \mathbf {g} _ {i} (\theta_ {0}) + \mathbf {G} _ {n} (\bar {\theta}) (\hat {\theta} - \theta_ {0}) \end{array}\tag{2.30}
$$

<sup>14</sup>Technically, $n ^ { - 1 } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } { ( x _ { i } - \mu ) } ^ { j } \overset { a . s . } {  } \mu _ { j }$ by the Kolmogorov law of large numbers, but since a.s. convergence implies convergence in probability, the original statement is also true. 

Theorem 2.9 (Mean Value Theorem). Let R be defined on a convex set $\Theta \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { k }$ . Further, let s be continuously differentiable on Θ with k by 1 gradient 

(2.29) 

Then for any points θ and there exists lying on the segment between $\theta$ and $\theta _ { 0 }$ such that $s ( \theta ) = s ( \theta _ { 0 } ) +$ where $\bar { \theta }$ is a vector that lies between $\hat { \boldsymbol { \theta } }$ and $\theta _ { 0 }$ , element-by-element. Note that $\begin{array} { r } { n ^ { - 1 } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } \mathbf { g } _ { i } ( \hat { \boldsymbol { \theta } } ) = \mathbf { 0 } } \end{array}$ by construction and so 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & n ^ {- 1} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \mathbf {g} _ {i} (\theta_ {0}) + \mathbf {G} _ {n} (\bar {\theta}) (\hat {\theta} - \theta_ {0}) = 0 \\ & \qquad \mathbf {G} _ {n} (\bar {\theta}) (\hat {\theta} - \theta_ {0}) = - n ^ {- 1} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \mathbf {g} _ {i} (\theta_ {0}) \\ & \qquad (\hat {\theta} - \theta_ {0}) = - \mathbf {G} _ {n} (\bar {\theta}) ^ {- 1} n ^ {- 1} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \mathbf {g} _ {i} (\theta_ {0}) \\ & \qquad \sqrt {n} (\hat {\theta} - \theta_ {0}) = - \mathbf {G} _ {n} (\bar {\theta}) ^ {- 1} \sqrt {n} n ^ {- 1} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \mathbf {g} _ {i} (\theta_ {0}) \\ & \qquad \sqrt {n} (\hat {\theta} - \theta_ {0}) = - \mathbf {G} _ {n} (\bar {\theta}) ^ {- 1} \sqrt {n} \mathbf {g} _ {n} (\theta_ {0}) \end{array}
$$

where $\begin{array} { r } { \mathbf { g } _ { n } ( \theta _ { 0 } ) = n ^ { - 1 } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } \mathbf { g } _ { i } ( \theta _ { 0 } ) } \end{array}$ is the average of the moment conditions. Thus the normalized difference between the estimated and the population values of the parameters, $\sqrt { n } \left( \hat { \boldsymbol { \theta } } - \boldsymbol { \theta } _ { 0 } \right)$ is equal to a scaled $\left( - \mathbf { G } _ { n } \left( { \bar { \theta } } \right) ^ { - 1 } \right)$ random variable $\left( { \sqrt { n } } \mathbf { g } _ { n } ( \theta _ { 0 } ) \right)$ that has an asymptotic normal distribution. By assumption $\sqrt { n } \mathbf { g } _ { n } ( \pmb { \theta } _ { 0 } ) \overset { d } {  } N ( 0 , \Sigma )$ and so 

$$
\sqrt {n} \left(\hat {\boldsymbol {\theta}} - \boldsymbol {\theta} _ {0}\right) \xrightarrow {d} N \left(\mathbf {0}, \mathbf {G} ^ {- 1} \Sigma \left(\mathbf {G} ^ {\prime}\right) ^ {- 1}\right)\tag{2.31}
$$

where ${ \bf G } _ { n } \left( \bar { \boldsymbol { \theta } } \right)$ has been replaced with its limit as $n  \infty , \mathbf { G }$ 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \mathbf {G} = \mathrm{plim} _ {n \to \infty} \left. \frac {\partial \mathbf {g} _ {n} (\theta)}{\partial \theta^ {\prime}} \right| _ {\theta = \theta_ {0}} \\ = \mathrm{plim} _ {n \to \infty} n ^ {- 1} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \left. \frac {\partial \mathbf {g} _ {i} (\theta)}{\partial \theta^ {\prime}} \right| _ {\theta = \theta_ {0}} \end{array}\tag{2.32}
$$

Since $\hat { \boldsymbol { \theta } }$ is a consistent estimator, $\hat { \boldsymbol { \theta } } \overset { \boldsymbol { P } } {  } \boldsymbol { \theta } _ { 0 }$ and so $\bar { \theta } \stackrel { p } {  } \theta _ { 0 }$ since it is between $\hat { \boldsymbol { \theta } }$ and $\theta _ { 0 }$ . This form of asymptotic covariance is known as a “sandwich” covariance estimator. 

## 2.4.1.1 Inference on the Mean and Variance

To estimate the mean and variance by the method of moments, two moment conditions are needed, 

$$
n ^ {- 1} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} X _ {i} = \hat {\mu}
$$

$$
n ^ {- 1} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} (X _ {i} - \hat {\mu}) ^ {2} = \hat {\sigma} ^ {2}
$$

## 2.4 Distribution Theory

To derive the asymptotic distribution, begin by forming $\mathbf { g } _ { i } .$ 

$$
\mathbf {g} _ {i} = \left[ \begin{array}{c} X _ {i} - \mu \\ (X _ {i} - \mu) ^ {2} - \sigma^ {2} \end{array} \right]
$$

Note that $\mathbf { g } _ { i }$ is mean $_ 0$ and a function of a single $x _ { i }$ so that $\mathbf { g } _ { i }$ is also i.i.d.. The covariance of $\mathbf { g } _ { i }$ is given by 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \Sigma = \operatorname{E} \left[ \mathbf {g} _ {i} \mathbf {g} _ {i} ^ {\prime} \right] = \operatorname{E} \left[ \left[ \begin{array}{c c} X _ {i} - \mu & \\ (X _ {i} - \mu) ^ {2} - \sigma^ {2} \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array}{c c} X _ {i} - \mu & (X _ {i} - \mu) ^ {2} - \sigma^ {2} \end{array} \right] \right] \\ = \operatorname{E} \left[ \begin{array}{c c} (X _ {i} - \mu) ^ {2} & (X _ {i} - \mu) ((X _ {i} - \mu) ^ {2} - \sigma^ {2}) \\ (X _ {i} - \mu) ((X _ {i} - \mu) ^ {2} - \sigma^ {2}) & ((X _ {i} - \mu) ^ {2} - \sigma^ {2}) ^ {2} \end{array} \right] \\ = \operatorname{E} \left[ \begin{array}{c c} (X _ {i} - \mu) ^ {2} & (X _ {i} - \mu) ^ {3} - \sigma^ {2} (X _ {i} - \mu) \\ (X _ {i} - \mu) ^ {3} - \sigma^ {2} (X _ {i} - \mu) & (X _ {i} - \mu) ^ {4} - 2 \sigma^ {2} (X _ {i} - \mu) ^ {2} + \sigma^ {4} \end{array} \right] \\ = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} \sigma^ {2} & \mu_ {3} \\ \mu_ {3} & \mu_ {4} - \sigma^ {4} \end{array} \right] \end{array}\tag{2.33}
$$

and the Jacobian is 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathbf {G} = \operatorname * {p l i m} _ {n \to \infty} n ^ {- 1} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \frac {\partial \mathbf {g} _ {i} (\theta)}{\partial \theta^ {\prime}} \bigg | _ {\theta = \theta_ {0}} \\ = \operatorname * {p l i m} _ {n \to \infty} n ^ {- 1} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \left[ \begin{array}{c c} - 1 & 0 \\ - 2 (X _ {i} - \mu) & - 1 \end{array} \right]. \end{array}
$$

Since p $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } n ^ { - 1 } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } \left( X _ { i } - \mu \right) = \operatorname { p l i m } _ { n \to \infty } \bar { x } _ { n } - \mu = 0 , } \end{array}$ 

$$
\mathbf {G} = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} - 1 & 0 \\ 0 & - 1 \end{array} \right].
$$

Thus, the asymptotic distribution of the method of moments estimator of $\theta = \left( \mu , \sigma ^ { 2 } \right) ^ { \prime }$ is 

$$
\sqrt {n} \left(\left[ \begin{array}{c} \hat {\mu} \\ \hat {\sigma} ^ {2} \end{array} \right] - \left[ \begin{array}{c} \mu \\ \sigma^ {2} \end{array} \right]\right) \stackrel {{d}} {{\to}} N \left(\left[ \begin{array}{c} 0 \\ 0 \end{array} \right], \left[ \begin{array}{c c} \sigma^ {2} & \mu_ {3} \\ \mu_ {3} & \mu_ {4} - \sigma^ {4} \end{array} \right]\right)
$$

since $\mathbf { G } = - \mathbf { I } _ { 2 }$ and so ${ \bf G } ^ { - 1 } \Sigma \left( { \bf G } ^ { - 1 } \right) ^ { \prime } = - { \bf I } _ { 2 } \Sigma \left( - { \bf I } _ { 2 } \right) = \Sigma .$ 

## 2.4.2 Maximum Likelihood

The steps to deriving the asymptotic distribution of an MLE are similar to those for a method of moments estimator. The key difference is that the score of the likelihood replaces the moment conditions. The maximum likelihood estimator is defined as the maximum of the log-likelihood of the data with respect to the parameters, 

$$
\hat {\theta} = \underset {\theta} {\arg \max} l (\theta ; \mathbf {y}).\tag{2.34}
$$

When the data are i.i.d., the log-likelihood can be factored into n log-likelihoods, one for each observation<sup>16</sup>, 

$$
l (\boldsymbol {\theta}; \mathbf {y}) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} l _ {i} (\boldsymbol {\theta}; y _ {i}).\tag{2.35}
$$

It is useful to work with the average log-likelihood directly, and so define 

$$
\bar {l} _ {n} (\theta ; \mathbf {y}) = n ^ {- 1} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} l _ {i} (\theta ; y _ {i}).\tag{2.36}
$$

The intuition behind the asymptotic distribution follows from the use of the average. Under some regularity conditions, ${ \bar { l } } _ { n } ( \theta ; \mathbf { y } )$ converges uniformly in $\theta$ to $\operatorname { E } \left[ l ( \theta ; y _ { i } ) \right]$ . However, since the average log-likelihood is becoming a good approximation for the expectation of the log-likelihood, the value of θ that maximizes the log-likelihood of the data and its expectation are very close for n sufficiently large. As a result,whenever the log-likelihood is differentiable and the range of $y _ { i }$ does not depend on any of the parameters in $\theta .$ 

$$
\mathrm{E} \left[ \frac {\partial \bar {l} _ {n} (\theta ; y _ {i})}{\partial \theta} \Bigg | _ {\theta = \theta_ {0}} \right] = \mathbf {0}\tag{2.37}
$$

where $\theta _ { 0 }$ are the parameters of the data generating process. This result follows since 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \int_ {\mathcal {S} _ {\mathbf {y}}} \frac {\partial \bar {l} _ {n} (\boldsymbol {\theta} _ {0} ; \mathbf {y})}{\partial \boldsymbol {\theta}} \bigg | _ {\boldsymbol {\theta} = \boldsymbol {\theta} _ {0}} f (\mathbf {y}; \boldsymbol {\theta} _ {0}) d y = \int_ {\mathcal {S} _ {\mathbf {y}}} \frac {\left. \frac {\partial f (\mathbf {y} ; \boldsymbol {\theta} _ {0})}{\partial \boldsymbol {\theta}} \right| _ {\boldsymbol {\theta} = \boldsymbol {\theta} _ {0}}}{f (\mathbf {y} ; \boldsymbol {\theta} _ {0})} f (\mathbf {y}; \boldsymbol {\theta} _ {0}) d y \\ = \int_ {\mathcal {S} _ {\mathbf {y}}} \frac {\partial f (\mathbf {y} ; \boldsymbol {\theta} _ {0})}{\partial \boldsymbol {\theta}} \bigg | _ {\boldsymbol {\theta} = \boldsymbol {\theta} _ {0}} d y \\ = \frac {\partial}{\partial \boldsymbol {\theta}} \int_ {\mathcal {S} _ {\mathbf {y}}} f (\mathbf {y}; \boldsymbol {\theta}) \bigg | _ {\boldsymbol {\theta} = \boldsymbol {\theta} _ {0}} d y \\ = \frac {\partial}{\partial \boldsymbol {\theta}} 1 \\ = 0 \end{array}\tag{2.38}
$$

where $\mathcal { S } _ { \mathbf { y } }$ denotes the support of $\mathbf { y } .$ . The scores of the average log-likelihood are 

$$
\frac {\partial \bar {l} _ {n} (\theta ; y _ {i})}{\partial \theta} = n ^ {- 1} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \frac {\partial l _ {i} (\theta ; y _ {i})}{\partial \theta}\tag{2.39}
$$

and when $Y _ { i }$ is i.i.d.then the scores are i.i.d., and the average scores follow a law of large numbers for θ close to $\theta _ { 0 }$ 

$$
n ^ {- 1} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \frac {\partial l _ {i} (\theta ; y _ {i})}{\partial \theta} \xrightarrow {a . s .} \mathrm{E} \left[ \frac {\partial l (\theta ; Y _ {i})}{\partial \theta} \right]\tag{2.40}
$$

As a result, the population value of $\theta , \theta _ { 0 }$ , also solves the first-order condition (asymptotically). The average scores are also the basis of the asymptotic normality of maximum likelihood estimators. Under some further regularity conditions, the average scores follow a central limit theorem, and so 

$$
\sqrt {n} \nabla_ {\theta} \bar {l} (\theta_ {0}) \equiv \sqrt {n} \left(n ^ {- 1} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \frac {\partial l (\theta ; y _ {i})}{\partial \theta}\right) \Bigg | _ {\theta = \theta_ {0}} \stackrel {{d}} {{\to}} N (\mathbf {0}, \mathcal {J}).\tag{2.41}
$$

Taking a mean value expansion around $\theta _ { 0 }$ , 

$$
\begin{array}{r l r} & & {\sqrt {n} \nabla_ {\theta} \bar {l} (\hat {\boldsymbol {\theta}}) = \sqrt {n} \nabla_ {\theta} \bar {l} (\boldsymbol {\theta} _ {0}) + \sqrt {n} \nabla_ {\theta \theta^ {\prime}} \bar {l} (\bar {\boldsymbol {\theta}}) (\hat {\boldsymbol {\theta}} - \boldsymbol {\theta} _ {0})} \\ & & {\mathbf {0} = \sqrt {n} \nabla_ {\theta} \bar {l} (\boldsymbol {\theta} _ {0}) + \sqrt {n} \nabla_ {\theta \theta^ {\prime}} \bar {l} (\bar {\boldsymbol {\theta}}) (\hat {\boldsymbol {\theta}} - \boldsymbol {\theta} _ {0})} \\ & & {- \sqrt {n} \nabla_ {\theta \theta^ {\prime}} \bar {l} (\bar {\boldsymbol {\theta}}) (\hat {\boldsymbol {\theta}} - \boldsymbol {\theta} _ {0}) = \sqrt {n} \nabla_ {\theta} \bar {l} (\boldsymbol {\theta} _ {0})} \\ & & {\sqrt {n} (\hat {\boldsymbol {\theta}} - \boldsymbol {\theta} _ {0}) = [ - \nabla_ {\theta \theta^ {\prime}} \bar {l} (\bar {\boldsymbol {\theta}}) ] ^ {- 1} \sqrt {n} \nabla_ {\theta} l (\boldsymbol {\theta} _ {0})} \end{array}
$$

where 

$$
\nabla_ {\theta \theta^ {\prime}} \bar {l} (\bar {\theta}) \equiv n ^ {- 1} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \frac {\partial^ {2} l (\theta ; y _ {i})}{\partial \theta \partial \theta^ {\prime}} \Bigg | _ {\theta = \bar {\theta}}\tag{2.42}
$$

and where $\bar { \theta }$ is a vector whose elements lie between $\hat { \boldsymbol { \theta } }$ and $\theta _ { 0 }$ . Since $\hat { \boldsymbol { \theta } }$ is a consistent estimator of $\theta _ { 0 } , \bar { \theta } \overset { p } {  } \theta _ { 0 }$ and so functions of $\bar { \theta }$ converge to their value at $\theta _ { 0 }$ , and the asymptotic distribution of the maximum likelihood estimator is 

$$
\sqrt {n} \left(\hat {\boldsymbol {\theta}} - \boldsymbol {\theta} _ {0}\right) \xrightarrow {d} N \left(\mathbf {0}, \mathcal {I} ^ {- 1} \mathcal {J I} ^ {- 1}\right)\tag{2.43}
$$

where 

$$
\mathcal {I} = - \mathrm{E} \left[ \left. \frac {\partial^ {2} l (\theta ; y _ {i})}{\partial \theta \partial \theta^ {\prime}} \right| _ {\theta = \theta_ {0}} \right]\tag{2.44}
$$

and 

$$
\mathcal {J} = \mathrm{E} \left[ \frac {\partial l (\theta ; y _ {i})}{\partial \theta} \frac {\partial l (\theta ; y _ {i})}{\partial \theta^ {\prime}} \Bigg | _ {\theta = \theta_ {0}} \right]\tag{2.45}
$$

The asymptotic covariance matrix can be further simplified using the information matrix equality, which states that $\mathcal { I } - \mathcal { I } \stackrel { p } {  }$ 0 and so 

$$
\sqrt {n} \left(\hat {\boldsymbol {\theta}} - \boldsymbol {\theta} _ {0}\right) \xrightarrow {d} N \left(\mathbf {0}, \mathcal {I} ^ {- 1}\right)\tag{2.46}
$$

or equivalently 

$$
\sqrt {n} \left(\hat {\boldsymbol {\theta}} - \boldsymbol {\theta} _ {0}\right) \xrightarrow {d} N \left(\mathbf {0}, \mathcal {J} ^ {- 1}\right).\tag{2.47}
$$

The information matrix equality follows from taking the derivative of the expected score, 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \frac {\partial^ {2} l (\boldsymbol {\theta} _ {0} ; \mathbf {y})}{\partial \boldsymbol {\theta} \partial \boldsymbol {\theta} ^ {\prime}} = \frac {1}{f (\mathbf {y} ; \boldsymbol {\theta})} \frac {\partial^ {2} f (\mathbf {y} ; \boldsymbol {\theta} _ {0})}{\partial \boldsymbol {\theta} \partial \boldsymbol {\theta} ^ {\prime}} - \frac {1}{f (\mathbf {y} ; \boldsymbol {\theta}) ^ {2}} \frac {\partial f (\mathbf {y} ; \boldsymbol {\theta} _ {0})}{\partial \boldsymbol {\theta}} \frac {\partial f (\mathbf {y} ; \boldsymbol {\theta} _ {0})}{\partial \boldsymbol {\theta} ^ {\prime}} \\ \frac {\partial^ {2} l (\boldsymbol {\theta} _ {0} ; \mathbf {y})}{\partial \boldsymbol {\theta} \partial \boldsymbol {\theta} ^ {\prime}} + \frac {\partial l (\boldsymbol {\theta} _ {0} ; \mathbf {y})}{\partial \boldsymbol {\theta}} \frac {\partial l (\boldsymbol {\theta} _ {0} ; \mathbf {y})}{\partial \boldsymbol {\theta} ^ {\prime}} = \frac {1}{f (\mathbf {y} ; \boldsymbol {\theta})} \frac {\partial^ {2} f (\mathbf {y} ; \boldsymbol {\theta} _ {0})}{\partial \boldsymbol {\theta} \partial \boldsymbol {\theta} ^ {\prime}} \end{array}\tag{2.48}
$$

and $\mathbf { S O } ,$ , when the model is correctly specified, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathrm{E} \left[ \frac {\partial^ {2} l (\boldsymbol {\theta} _ {0} ; \mathbf {y})}{\partial \theta \partial \theta^ {\prime}} + \frac {\partial l (\boldsymbol {\theta} _ {0} ; \mathbf {y})}{\partial \theta} \frac {\partial l (\boldsymbol {\theta} _ {0} ; \mathbf {y})}{\partial \theta^ {\prime}} \right] = \int_ {\mathcal {S} _ {\mathbf {y}}} \frac {1}{f (\mathbf {y} ; \boldsymbol {\theta})} \frac {\partial^ {2} f (\mathbf {y} ; \boldsymbol {\theta} _ {0})}{\partial \theta \partial \theta^ {\prime}} f (\mathbf {y}; \boldsymbol {\theta}) d \mathbf {y} \\ = \int_ {\mathcal {S} _ {\mathbf {y}}} \frac {\partial^ {2} f (\mathbf {y} ; \boldsymbol {\theta} _ {0})}{\partial \theta \partial \theta^ {\prime}} d \mathbf {y} \\ = \frac {\partial^ {2}}{\partial \theta \partial \theta^ {\prime}} \int_ {\mathcal {S} _ {\mathbf {y}}} f (\mathbf {y}; \boldsymbol {\theta} _ {0}) d \mathbf {y} \\ = \frac {\partial^ {2}}{\partial \theta \partial \theta^ {\prime}} 1 \\ = 0. \end{array}
$$

and 

$$
\operatorname{E} \left[ \frac {\partial^ {2} l (\boldsymbol {\theta} _ {0} ; \mathbf {y})}{\partial \boldsymbol {\theta} \partial \boldsymbol {\theta} ^ {\prime}} \right] = - \operatorname{E} \left[ \frac {\partial l (\boldsymbol {\theta} _ {0} ; \mathbf {y})}{\partial \boldsymbol {\theta}} \frac {\partial l (\boldsymbol {\theta} _ {0} ; \mathbf {y})}{\partial \boldsymbol {\theta} ^ {\prime}} \right].
$$

A related concept, and one which applies to ML estimators when the information matrix equality holds, at least asymptotically, is the Cramér-Rao lower bound. 

Theorem 2.10 (Cramér-Rao Inequality). Let $f ( \mathbf { y } ; \theta )$ be the joint density of y where θ is a k dimensional parameter vector. Let $\hat { \boldsymbol { \theta } }$ be a consistent estimator of θ with finite covariance. Under some regularity condition on $f ( \cdot )$ 

$$
\operatorname{avar} (\hat {\boldsymbol {\theta}}) \geq \mathcal {I} ^ {- 1} (\boldsymbol {\theta})\tag{2.49}
$$

where 

$$
\mathcal {I} (\boldsymbol {\theta}) = - \mathrm{E} \left[ \left. \frac {\partial^ {2} \ln f (Y _ {i} ; \boldsymbol {\theta})}{\partial \boldsymbol {\theta} \partial \boldsymbol {\theta} ^ {\prime}} \right| _ {\boldsymbol {\theta} = \boldsymbol {\theta} _ {0}} \right].\tag{2.50}
$$

The important implication of the Cramér-Rao theorem is that maximum likelihood estimators, which are generally consistent, are asymptotically efficient.<sup>17</sup> This guarantee makes a strong case for using the maximum likelihood when available. 

## 2.4.2.1 Inference in a Poisson MLE

Recall that the log-likelihood in a Poisson MLE is 

$$
l (\lambda ; \mathbf {y}) = - n \lambda + \ln (\lambda) \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} Y _ {i} - \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {y _ {i}} \ln (i)
$$

and that the first-order condition is 

$$
\frac {\partial l (\lambda ; \mathbf {y})}{\partial \lambda} = - n + \lambda^ {- 1} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} Y _ {i}.
$$

The MLE was previously shown to be $\hat { \lambda } = n ^ { - 1 } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } y _ { i }$ . To compute the variance, take the expectation of the negative of the second derivative, 

$$
\frac {\partial^ {2} l (\lambda ; Y _ {i})}{\partial \lambda^ {2}} = - \lambda^ {- 2} Y _ {i}
$$

and so 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \mathcal {I} = - \mathrm{E} \left[ \frac {\partial^ {2} l (\lambda ; Y _ {i})}{\partial \lambda^ {2}} \right] & = - \mathrm{E} \left[ - \lambda^ {- 2} Y _ {i} \right] \\ & = \left[ \lambda^ {- 2} \mathrm{E} [ Y _ {i} ] \right] \\ & = \left[ \lambda^ {- 2} \lambda \right] \\ & = \left[ \frac {\lambda}{\lambda^ {2}} \right] \\ & = \lambda^ {- 1} \end{array}
$$

and so $\sqrt { n } \left( \hat { \lambda } - \lambda _ { 0 } \right) \stackrel { d } { \to } N \left( 0 , \lambda \right)$ since ${ \mathcal { T } } ^ { - 1 } = \lambda$ 

Alternatively the covariance of the scores could be used to compute the parameter covariance, 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \mathcal {J} & = & \mathrm{V} \left[ \left(- 1 + \frac {Y _ {i}}{\lambda}\right) ^ {2} \right] \\ & = & \frac {1}{\lambda^ {2}} \mathrm{V} [ Y _ {i} ] \\ & = & \lambda^ {- 1}. \end{array}
$$

$\mathcal { T } \equiv \mathcal { T }$ and so the IME holds when the data are Poisson distributed. If the data were not Poisson distributed, then it would not normally be the case that E $\mathbf { \nabla } [ Y _ { i } ] = \mathbf { V } \left[ Y _ { i } \right] = \lambda$ , and so $\mathcal { T }$ and $\mathcal { I }$ would not (generally) be equal. 

## 2.4.2.2 Inference in the Normal (Gaussian) MLE

Recall that the MLE estimators of the mean and variance are 

$$
\hat {\mu} = n ^ {- 1} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} Y _ {i}
$$

$$
\hat {\sigma} ^ {2} = n ^ {- 1} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} (Y _ {i} - \hat {\mu}) ^ {2}
$$

and that the log-likelihood is 

$$
l (\theta ; \mathbf {y}) = - \frac {n}{2} \ln (2 \pi) - \frac {n}{2} \ln (\sigma^ {2}) - \frac {1}{2} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \frac {(Y _ {i} - \mu) ^ {2}}{\sigma^ {2}}.
$$

Taking the derivative with respect to the parameter vector, $\theta = \left( \mu , \sigma ^ { 2 } \right) ^ { \prime }$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {\partial l (\theta ; \mathbf {y})}{\partial \mu} = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \frac {(Y _ {i} - \mu)}{\sigma^ {2}} \\ \frac {\partial l (\theta ; \mathbf {y})}{\partial \sigma^ {2}} = - \frac {n}{2 \sigma^ {2}} + \frac {1}{2} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \frac {(Y _ {i} - \mu) ^ {2}}{\sigma^ {4}}. \end{array}
$$

The second derivatives are 

$$
\frac {\partial^ {2} l (\boldsymbol {\theta} ; \mathbf {y})}{\partial \mu \partial \mu} = - \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \frac {1}{\sigma^ {2}}
$$

$$
\frac {\partial^ {2} l (\boldsymbol {\theta} ; \mathbf {y})}{\partial \mu \partial \sigma^ {2}} = - \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \frac {(Y _ {i} - \mu)}{\sigma^ {4}}
$$

$$
\frac {\partial^ {2} l (\boldsymbol {\theta} ; \mathbf {y})}{\partial \sigma^ {2} \partial \sigma^ {2}} = \frac {n}{2 \sigma^ {4}} - \frac {2}{2} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \frac {(Y _ {i} - \mu) ^ {2}}{\sigma^ {6}}.
$$

The first does not depend on data and so no expectation is needed. The other two have expectations, 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \mathrm{E} \left[ \frac {\partial^ {2} l (\theta ; y _ {i})}{\partial \mu \partial \sigma^ {2}} \right] & = \mathrm{E} \left[ - \frac {(Y _ {i} - \mu)}{\sigma^ {4}} \right] \\ & = - \frac {(\mathrm{E} [ Y _ {i} ] - \mu)}{\sigma^ {4}} \\ & = - \frac {\mu - \mu}{\sigma^ {4}} \\ & = 0 \end{array}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \mathrm{E} \left[ \frac {\partial^ {2} l (\theta ; y _ {i})}{\partial \sigma^ {2} \partial \sigma^ {2}} \right] & = \mathrm{E} \left[ \frac {1}{2 \sigma^ {4}} - \frac {2}{2} \frac {(Y _ {i} - \mu) ^ {2}}{\sigma^ {6}} \right] \\ & = \frac {1}{2 \sigma^ {4}} - \frac {\mathrm{E} \left[ (Y _ {i} - \mu) ^ {2} \right]}{\sigma^ {6}} \\ & = \frac {1}{2 \sigma^ {4}} - \frac {\sigma^ {2}}{\sigma^ {6}} \\ & = \frac {1}{2 \sigma^ {4}} - \frac {1}{\sigma^ {4}} \\ & = - \frac {1}{2 \sigma^ {4}} \end{array}
$$

Putting these together, the expected Hessian can be formed, 

$$
\operatorname{E} \left[ \frac {\partial^ {2} l (\theta ; y _ {i})}{\partial \theta \partial \theta^ {\prime}} \right] = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} - \frac {1}{\sigma^ {2}} & 0 \\ 0 & - \frac {1}{2 \sigma^ {4}} \end{array} \right]
$$

and so the asymptotic covariance is 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \mathcal {I} ^ {- 1} = - \mathrm{E} \left[ \frac {\partial^ {2} l (\theta ; y _ {i})}{\partial \theta \partial \theta^ {\prime}} \right] ^ {- 1} & = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} \frac {1}{\sigma^ {2}} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac {1}{2 \sigma^ {4}} \end{array} \right] ^ {- 1} \\ & = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} \sigma^ {2} & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \sigma^ {4} \end{array} \right] \end{array}
$$

The asymptotic distribution is then 

$$
\sqrt {n} \left(\left[ \begin{array}{c} \hat {\mu} \\ \hat {\sigma} ^ {2} \end{array} \right] - \left[ \begin{array}{c} \mu \\ \sigma^ {2} \end{array} \right]\right) \stackrel {{d}} {{\to}} N \left(\left[ \begin{array}{c} 0 \\ 0 \end{array} \right], \left[ \begin{array}{c c} \sigma^ {2} & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \sigma^ {4} \end{array} \right]\right)
$$

Note that this is different from the asymptotic variance for the method of moments estimator of the mean and the variance. This is because the data have been assumed to come from a normal distribution and so the MLE is correctly specified. As a result $\mu _ { 3 } = 0$ (the normal is symmetric) and the IME holds. In general the IME does not hold and so the asymptotic covariance may take a different form which depends on the moments of the data as in eq. (2.33). 

## 2.4.3 Quasi Maximum Likelihood

While maximum likelihood is an appealing estimation approach, it has one important drawback: knowledge of $f \left( \mathbf { y } ; \theta \right)$ . In practice the density assumed in maximum likelihood estimation, $f \left( \mathbf { y } ; \theta \right)$ , is misspecified for the actual density of $\mathbf { y } , g \left( \mathbf { y } \right)$ . This case has been widely studied, and estimators where the distribution is misspecified are known as quasi-maximum likelihood (QML) estimators. QML estimators generally lose all of the features that make maximum likelihood estimators so appealing: they are generally inconsistent for the parameters of interest; the information matrix equality does not hold; and they do not achieve the Cramér-Rao lower bound. 

First, consider the expected score from a QML estimator, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathrm{E} _ {g} \left[ \frac {\partial l (\theta_ {0} ; \mathbf {y})}{\partial \theta} \right] = \int_ {\mathcal {S} _ {\mathbf {y}}} \frac {\partial l (\theta_ {0} ; \mathbf {y})}{\partial \theta} g (\mathbf {y}) d y \\ = \int_ {\mathcal {S} _ {\mathbf {y}}} \frac {\partial l (\theta_ {0} ; \mathbf {y})}{\partial \theta} \frac {f (\mathbf {y} ; \theta_ {0})}{f (\mathbf {y} ; \theta_ {0})} g (\mathbf {y}) d y \\ = \int_ {\mathcal {S} _ {\mathbf {y}}} \frac {\partial l (\theta_ {0} ; \mathbf {y})}{\partial \theta} \frac {g (\mathbf {y})}{f (\mathbf {y} ; \theta_ {0})} f (\mathbf {y}; \theta_ {0}) d y \\ = \int_ {\mathcal {S} _ {\mathbf {y}}} h (\mathbf {y}) \frac {\partial l (\theta_ {0} ; \mathbf {y})}{\partial \theta} f (\mathbf {y}; \theta_ {0}) d y \end{array}\tag{2.51}
$$

which shows that the QML estimator can be seen as a weighted average with respect to the density assumed. These weights depend on the data, and so it is no longer be the case that the expectation of the score at $\theta _ { 0 }$ is necessarily be 0. Instead QML estimators generally converge to another value of $\theta$ , $\theta ^ { * }$ , that depends on both $f \left( \cdot \right)$ and $g \left( \cdot \right)$ and is known as the pseudo-true value of θ. 

The other important consideration when using QML to estimate parameters is that the Information Matrix Equality (IME) no longer holds, and so “sandwich” covariance estimators must be used, and likelihood ratio statistics do not have standard $\chi ^ { 2 }$ distributions. An alternative interpretation of a QML estimator is that of a method of moments estimator where the scores of $l \left( \boldsymbol { \theta } ; \mathbf { y } \right)$ are used to choose the moments. With this interpretation, the distribution theory of the method of moments estimator applies as long as the scores, evaluated at the pseudo-true parameters, follow a CLT.

Figure 2.4 contains three distributions (left column) and the asymptotic covariance of the mean and the variance estimators, illustrated through joint confidence ellipses containing 80, 95, and 99% prob ability that the true value is within their bounds (right column).<sup>18</sup> The ellipses were all derived from the asymptotic covariance of $\hat { \mu }$ and $\hat { \sigma } ^ { 2 }$ where the data are i.i.d.and distributed according to a mixture ofnormals distribution where 

$$
Y _ {i} = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \mu_ {1} + \sigma_ {1} Z _ {i} & \text { with   probability } p \\ \mu_ {2} + \sigma_ {2} Z _ {i} & \text { with   probability } 1 - p \end{array} \right.
$$

where $z$ is a standard normal. A mixture of normals is constructed from mixing draws from a finite set of normals with possibly different means and variances and can take a wide variety of shapes. All of the variables were constructed so that $\operatorname { E } \left[ Y _ { i } \right] = 0$ and $\mathrm { V } \left[ Y _ { i } \right] = 1$ . This restriction requires 

$$
p \mu_ {1} + (1 - p) \mu_ {2} = 0
$$

and

p \left(\mu_ {1} ^ {2} + \sigma_ {1} ^ {2}\right) + (1 - p) \left(\mu_ {2} ^ {2} + \sigma_ {2} ^ {2}\right) = 1.
$$

The values used to produce the figures are listed in table 2.1. The first set is simply a standard normal since $p = 1$ . The second is known as a contaminated normal and is composed of a frequently occurring (95% of the time) mean-zero normal with variance slightly smaller than 1 (.8), contaminated by a rare but high variance (4.8) mean-zero normal. This mixture produces heavy tails but does not result in a skewed distribution. The final example uses different means and variance to produce a right (positively) skewed distribution. 

The confidence ellipses illustrated in figure 2.4 are all derived from estimators produced assuming that the data are normally distributed, but using the “sandwich” version of the covariance, ${ \cal T } ^ { - 1 } { \mathcal { I } } { \cal T } ^ { - 1 }$ The top panel illustrates the correctly specified maximum likelihood estimator. Here the confidence ellipse is symmetric about its center. This shape occurs when the parameters are uncorrelated – and hence independent since they are asymptotically normal – but have different variances. The middle panel has a similar shape but is elongated on the variance axis (x). This example illustrates that the asymptotic variance of $\hat { \sigma } ^ { 2 }$ is affected by the heavy tails of the data (large $4 ^ { \mathrm { { \hat { t h } } } }$ moment) of the contaminated normal. The final confidence ellipse is rotated, reflecting that the mean and variance estimators are no longer asymptotically independent. These final two cases are examples of QML; the estimator is derived assuming a normal distribution, but the data are not. In these examples, the estimators are still consistent but have different covariances.<sup>19</sup>
