Figure 4.11: These six panels contain the standard HP filter, the $B K _ { 1 2 } ( 6 , 3 2 )$ filter, the first difference filter, an EWMA with $\lambda = . 9 4 ,$ , a MACD(12,26) and the difference between a 20-day and a 50-day moving average. The gain functions in the right hand column have been normalized so that the maximum weight is 1. The is equivalent to scaling all of the filter weights by a constant, and so is simple a change in variance of the filter output.


BN decomposition is simple: if the predictable part of the long-run component places the long-run component above its current value, then the cyclic component should be negative. Similarly, if the predictable part of the long-run component expects that the long-run component should trend lower, then the cyclic component should be positive. Formally the BN decomposition is defined as 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \tau_ {t} = \lim _ {h \to \infty} \hat {Y} _ {t + h | t} - h \mu \\ C _ {t} = Y _ {t} - \tau_ {t} \end{array}\tag{4.102}
$$

where $\mu$ is the drift in the trend, if any. The trend can be equivalently expressed as the current level of $Y _ { t }$ plus the expected increments minus the drift, 

$$
\tau_ {t} = Y _ {t} + \lim _ {h \rightarrow \infty} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {h} \mathrm{E} \left[ \Delta \hat {Y} _ {t + i | t} - \mu \right]\tag{4.103}
$$

where $\mu$ is the unconditional expectation of the increments to $Y _ { t } , \mathrm { E } [ \Delta \hat { Y } _ { t + j | t } ]$ . The trend component contains the persistent component, and so the filter applied must be a low-pass filter, while the cyclic component is stationary and so must be the output of a high-pass filter. The gain of the filter applied when using the BN decomposition depends crucially on the forecasting model for the short-run component. 

Suppose $\left\{ Y _ { t } \right\}$ is an I(1) series which has both a permanent and transitive component. Since $\left\{ Y _ { t } \right\}$ is I(1), $\Delta Y _ { t }$ must be I(0) and so can be described by a stationary ARMA(P,Q) process. For simplicity, suppose that $\Delta Y _ { t }$ follows an MA(3) so that 

$$
\Delta Y _ {t} = \phi_ {0} + \theta_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 1} + \theta_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 2} + \theta_ {3} \varepsilon_ {t - 3} + \varepsilon_ {t}
$$

In this model, $\mu = \phi _ { 0 }$ , and the h-step ahead forecast is given by 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \Delta \hat {Y} _ {t + 1 | t} = \mu + \theta_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t} + \theta_ {2} \varepsilon_ {t - 1} + \theta_ {3} \varepsilon_ {t - 2} \\ \Delta \hat {Y} _ {t + 2 | t} = \mu + \theta_ {2} \varepsilon_ {t} + \theta_ {3} \varepsilon_ {t - 1} \\ \Delta \hat {Y} _ {t + 3 | t} = \mu + \theta_ {3} \varepsilon_ {t} \\ \Delta \hat {Y} _ {t + h | t} = \mu h \geq 4, \end{array}
$$

and so 

$$
\tau_ {t} = Y _ {t} + \left(\theta_ {1} + \theta_ {2} + \theta_ {3}\right) \varepsilon_ {t} + \left(\theta_ {2} + \theta_ {3}\right) \varepsilon_ {t - 1} + \theta_ {3} \varepsilon_ {t - 2}
$$

and 

$$
C _ {t} = - \left(\theta_ {1} + \theta_ {2} + \theta_ {3}\right) \varepsilon_ {t} - \left(\theta_ {2} + \theta_ {3}\right) \varepsilon_ {t - 1} - \theta_ {3} \varepsilon_ {t - 2}.
$$

Alternatively, suppose that $\Delta Y _ { t }$ follows an AR(1) so that 

$$
\Delta Y _ {t} = \phi_ {0} + \phi_ {1} \Delta Y _ {t - 1} + \varepsilon_ {t}.
$$

This model can be equivalently defined in terms of deviations around the long-run mean, $\Delta \tilde { y } _ { t } = \Delta Y _ { t } -$ $\phi _ { 0 } / ( 1 - \phi _ { 1 } )$ , as 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \Delta Y _ {t} = \phi_ {0} + \phi_ {1} \Delta Y _ {t - 1} + \varepsilon_ {t} \\ \Delta Y _ {t} = \phi_ {0} \frac {1 - \phi_ {1}}{1 - \phi_ {1}} + \phi_ {1} \Delta Y _ {t - 1} + \varepsilon_ {t} \\ \Delta Y _ {t} = \frac {\phi_ {0}}{1 - \phi_ {1}} - \phi_ {1} \frac {\phi_ {0}}{1 - \phi_ {1}} + \phi_ {1} \Delta Y _ {t - 1} + \varepsilon_ {t} \\ \Delta Y _ {t} - \frac {\phi_ {0}}{1 - \phi_ {1}} = \phi_ {1} \left(\Delta Y _ {t - 1} - \frac {\phi_ {0}}{1 - \phi_ {1}}\right) + \varepsilon_ {t} \\ \Delta \tilde {y} _ {t} = \phi_ {1} \Delta \tilde {y} _ {t - 1} + \varepsilon_ {t}. \end{array}
$$

In this transformed model, $\mu = 0$ which simplifies finding the expression for the trend. The h-step ahead forecast if $\Delta \tilde { y } _ { t }$ is given by 

$$
\Delta \hat {\tilde {y}} _ {t + h | t} = \phi_ {1} ^ {h} \Delta \tilde {y} _ {t}
$$

and so 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \tau_ {t} = Y _ {t} + \lim _ {h \to \infty} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {h} \Delta \hat {\tilde {y}} _ {t + i | t} \\ = Y _ {t} + \lim _ {h \to \infty} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {h} \phi_ {1} ^ {i} \Delta \tilde {y} _ {t} \\ = Y _ {t} + \lim _ {h \to \infty} \Delta \tilde {y} _ {t} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {h} \phi_ {1} ^ {i} \\ = Y _ {t} + \lim _ {h \to \infty} \Delta \tilde {y} _ {t} \frac {\phi_ {1}}{1 - \phi_ {1}} \end{array}
$$

which follows since $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { h \to \infty } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { h } \phi _ { 1 } ^ { i } = - 1 + \operatorname* { l i m } _ { h \to \infty } \sum _ { i = 0 } ^ { h } \phi _ { 1 } ^ { i } = 1 / \big ( 1 - \phi _ { 1 } \big ) - 1 } \end{array}$ . The main criticism of the Beveridge-Nelson decomposition is that the trend and the cyclic component are perfectly (negatively) correlation. 

## 4.12.7 Extracting the cyclic components from Real US GDP

The cyclic component was extracted from log real US GDP data taken from the Federal Reserve Economics Database using alternative filters. Data were available from 1947 Q1 to Q2 2020. Figure 4.12 contains the cyclical component extracted using four methods. The top panel contains the standard HP filter with $\lambda = 1 6 0 0$ The middle panel contains $B K _ { 1 2 } ( 6 , 3 2 )$ (solid) and $B K _ { 1 2 } ( 1 , 3 2 )$ (dashed) filters, the latter of which is a high pass-filter since the faster frequency is 1. Note that the first and last 12 points of the cyclic component are set to 0. The bottom panel contains the cyclic component extracted using a Beveridge-Nelson decomposition based on an $\operatorname { A R } ( 1 )$ estimated on GDP growth data. For the BN decomposition, the first 2 points are zero, reflecting the loss of data due to the first difference and fitting the AR(1) to the first difference.<sup>20</sup> 

The HP filter and the $B K _ { 1 2 } ( 1 , 3 2 )$ are remarkably similar with a correlation of over 99%. The correlation between the $B K _ { 1 2 } ( 6 , 3 2 )$ and the HP filter is 96%. The key difference between the two is in the lack of a high-frequency component in the HP filter. The cyclic component from the BN decomposition has a small negative correlation with the other three filters, although choosing a different model for GDP growth would change the decomposition. 

## 4.13 Nonlinear Models for Time-Series Analysis

While this chapter has exclusively focused on linear time-series processes, many non-linear timeseries processes have been found to provide parsimonious descriptions of the dynamics in financial data. Two which have proven particularly useful in the analysis of financial data are Markov Switching Autoregressions (MSAR) and Threshold Autoregressions (TAR), especially the subclass of Self-Exciting Threshold Autoregressions (SETAR).<sup>21</sup>

## 4.13.1 Markov Switching Autoregression

Markov switching autoregression, introduced into econometrics in Hamilton (1989), uses a composite model which evolves according to both an autoregression and a latent state which determines the value of the autoregressive parameters. In financial applications using low-frequency asset returns, an MSAR that allows the mean and the variance to be state-dependent has been found to outperform linear models (Perez-Quiros and Timmermann, 2000). 

Definition 4.45 (Markov Switching Autoregression). A k-state Markov switching autoregression (MSAR) is a stochastic process which has dynamics that evolve through both a Markovian state process and an autoregression where the autoregressive parameters are state dependent. The states, labeled $1 , 2 , \ldots , k ,$ , are denoted $s _ { t }$ and follow a k-state latent Markov Chain with transition matrix P, 

$$
\mathbf {P} = \left[ \begin{array}{c c c c} p _ {1 1} & p _ {1 2} & \dots & p _ {1 k} \\ p _ {2 1} & p _ {2 2} & \dots & p _ {2 k} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\ p _ {k 1} & p _ {k 2} & \dots & p _ {k k} \end{array} \right]\tag{4.104}
$$

where $p _ { i j } = P r ( s _ { t + 1 } = i | s _ { t } = j )$ . Note that the columns must sum to 1 since $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { k } P r ( s _ { t + 1 } = i | s _ { t } = } \end{array}$ $j ) = 1$ . Data are generated according to a $\mathrm { P ^ { t h } }$ order autoregression, 

$$
Y _ {t} = \phi_ {0} ^ {(s _ {t})} + \phi_ {1} ^ {(s _ {t})} Y _ {t - 1} + \ldots + \phi_ {P} ^ {(s _ {t})} Y _ {t - p} + \sigma^ {(s _ {t})} \varepsilon_ {t}\tag{4.105}
$$

where ${ \boldsymbol { \phi } } ^ { ( s _ { t } ) } = [ \phi _ { 0 } ^ { ( s _ { t } ) } \phi _ { 1 } ^ { ( s _ { t } ) } \ldots \phi _ { P } ^ { ( s _ { t } ) } ] ^ { \prime }$ are state-dependent autoregressive parameters, $\pmb { \sigma } ^ { ( s _ { t } ) }$ is the statedependent standard deviation and $\varepsilon _ { t } \stackrel { \mathrm { i . i . } } { \sim } N ( 0 , 1 ) . \stackrel { 2 2 }  $ The unconditional state probabilities $( \mathrm { P r } \big ( s _ { t } = i \big ) )$ , known as the ergodic probabilities, are denoted ${ \pmb \pi } = [ \pi _ { 1 } \pi _ { 2 } \ldots \pi _ { k } ] ^ { \prime }$ and are the solution to 

$$
\pi = \mathbf {P} \pi .\tag{4.106}
$$

The ergodic probabilities can also be computed as the normalized eigenvector of P corresponding to the only unit eigenvalue. 

Rather than attempting to derive properties of an MSAR, consider a simple specification with two states, no autoregressive terms, and where only the mean of the process varies<sup>23</sup> 

$$
Y _ {t} = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \phi^ {H} + \varepsilon_ {t} \\ \phi^ {L} + \varepsilon_ {t} \end{array} \right.\tag{4.107}
$$

where the two states are indexed by H (high) and L (low). The transition matrix is 

$$
\mathbf {P} = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} p _ {H H} & p _ {H L} \\ p _ {L H} & p _ {L L} \end{array} \right] = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} p _ {H H} & 1 - p _ {L L} \\ 1 - p _ {H H} & p _ {L L} \end{array} \right]\tag{4.108}
$$

and the unconditional probabilities of being in the high and low state, $\pi _ { H }$ and $\pi _ { L }$ , respectively, are 

$$
\pi_ {H} = \frac {1 - p _ {L L}}{2 - p _ {H H} - p _ {L L}}\tag{4.109}
$$

$$
\pi_ {L} = \frac {1 - p _ {H H}}{2 - p _ {H H} - p _ {L L}}.\tag{4.110}
$$

This simple model is useful for understanding the data generation in a Markov Switching process: 

1. At $t = 0$ an initial state, $s _ { 0 }$ , is chosen according to the ergodic (unconditional) probabilities. With probability $\pi _ { H } , s _ { 0 } = H$ and with probability $\pi _ { L } = 1 - \pi _ { H } , s _ { 0 } = L$ 

2. The state probabilities evolve independently from the observed data according to a Markov Chain. If $s _ { 0 } = H , s _ { 1 } = H$ with probability p<sub>HH</sub>, the probability $s _ { t + 1 } = H$ given $s _ { t } = H$ and $s _ { 1 } = L$ with probability $p _ { L H } = 1 - p _ { H H }$ . If $s _ { 0 } = L , s _ { 1 } = H$ with probability $p _ { H L } = 1 - p _ { L L }$ and $s _ { 1 } = L$ with probability $p _ { L L }$ 

3. Once the state at $t = 1$ is known, the value of $Y _ { 1 }$ is chosen according to 

$$
Y _ {1} = \left\{ \begin{array}{c l} \phi^ {H} + \varepsilon_ {1} & \text { if } s _ {1} = H \\ \phi^ {L} + \varepsilon_ {t} & \text { if } s _ {1} = L \end{array} \right..
$$

4. Steps 2 and 3 are repeated for $t = 2 , 3 , . . . , T$ , to produce a time series of Markov Switching data. 

## 4.13.1.1 Markov Switching Examples

Using the 2-state Markov Switching Autoregression described above, four systems were simulated for 100 observations. 

• Pure mixture 

$$
\begin{array}{l} - \mu_ {H} = 4, \mu_ {L} = - 2, \mathrm{V} [ \varepsilon_ {t} ] = 1 \text { in   both   states } \\ - p _ {H H} = . 5 = p _ {L L} \\ - \pi_ {H} = \pi_ {L} = . 5 \end{array}
$$

– Remark: This is a “pure” mixture model where the probability of each state does not depend on the past. This occurs because the probability of going from high to high is the same as the probability of going from low to high, 0.5. 

• Two persistent States 

– µ<sub>H</sub> = 4, µ<sub>L</sub> = 2, V[ε<sub>t</sub>] = 1 in both states 

$p _ { H H } = . 9 = p _ { L L }$ so the average duration of each state is 10 periods. 

$$
- \pi_ {H} = \pi_ {L} = . 5
$$

– Remark: Unlike the first parameterization this is not a simple mixture. Conditional on the current state being H, there is a 90% chance that the next state will remain H. 

• One persistent state, on transitory state 

$$
\begin{array}{l} - \mu_ {H} = 4, \mu_ {L} = - 2, \mathrm{V} [ \varepsilon_ {t} ] = 1 \text {   if   } s _ {t} = H \text {   and   } \mathrm{V} [ \varepsilon_ {t} ] = 2 \text {   if   } s _ {t} = L \\ - p _ {H H} = . 9, p _ {L L} = . 5 \\ - \pi_ {H} = . 8 3, \pi_ {L} = . 1 6 \end{array}
$$

– Remark: This type of model is consistent with quarterly data on U.S. GDP where booms (H) typically last 10 quarters while recessions die quickly, typically in 2 quarters. 

• Mixture with different variances 

$$
- \mu_ {H} = 4, \mu_ {L} = - 2, \mathrm{V} [ \varepsilon_ {t} ] = 1 \text {   if   } s _ {t} = H \text {   and   } \mathrm{V} [ \varepsilon_ {t} ] = 1 6 \text {   if   } s _ {t} = L
$$

$$
- p _ {H H} = . 5 = p _ {L L}
$$

$$
\pi_ {H} = \pi_ {L} = . 5
$$

– Remark: This is another “pure” mixture model, but the variances differ between the states. One nice feature of mixture models (MSAR is a member of the family of mixture models) is that the unconditional distribution of the data may be non-normal even though the shocks are conditionally normally distributed.<sup>24</sup> 

Figure 4.13 contains plots of 100 data points generated from each of these processes. The first (MSAR(1)) produces a mixture with modes at -2 and 4 each with equal probability, and the states (top panel, bottom right) are i.i.d.. The second process produced a similar unconditional distribution, but the state evolution is very different. Each state is very persistent and, conditional on the current state being high or low, the next state is likely to remain the same. The third process had one very persistent state and one with much less persistence. These dynamics produced a large skew in the unconditional distribution since the state where $\mu = - 2$ was visited less frequently than the state with $\mu = 4$ . The final process (MSAR(4)) has state dynamics similar to the first but produces a very different unconditional distribution. The difference occurs since the variance depends on the state of the Markov process. 

## 4.13.2 Threshold Autoregression and Self-Exciting Threshold Autoregression

A second class of nonlinear models that have gained considerable traction in financial applications are Threshold Autoregressions (TAR), and in particular, the subfamily of Self-Exciting Threshold Autoregressions (SETAR).<sup>25</sup> 

Definition 4.46 (Threshold Autoregression). A threshold autoregression is a $\mathrm { P ^ { t h } }$ Order autoregressive process with state-dependent parameters where the state is determined by the lagged level of an exogenous variable $X _ { t - k }$ for some $k \geq 1$ 

$$
Y _ {t} = \phi_ {0} ^ {(s _ {t})} + \phi_ {1} ^ {(s _ {t})} Y _ {t - 1} + \dots + \phi_ {P} ^ {(s _ {t})} Y _ {t - p} + \sigma^ {(s _ {t})} \varepsilon_ {t}\tag{4.111}
$$

Let $- \infty = X _ { 0 } < X _ { 1 } < X _ { 2 } < \ldots < X _ { N } < X _ { N + 1 } = \infty$ be a partition of x in to $N + 1$ distinct bins. $s _ { t } = j$ if $X _ { t - k } \in ( x _ { j } , x _ { j + 1 } )$ 

Self-exciting threshold autoregressions, introduced in Tong (1978), are similarly defined. The only change is in the definition of the threshold variable; rather than relying on an exogenous variable to determine the state, the state in SETARs is determined by lagged values of the dependent variable. 

Definition 4.47 (Self Exciting Threshold Autoregression). A self exciting threshold autoregression is a $\mathrm { P ^ { t h } }$ Order autoregressive process with state-dependent parameters where the state is determined by the lagged level of the dependent variable, $Y _ { t - k }$ for some $k \geq 1$ 

$$
Y _ {t} = \phi_ {0} ^ {(s _ {t})} + \phi_ {1} ^ {(s _ {t})} Y _ {t - 1} + \ldots + \phi_ {P} ^ {(s _ {t})} Y _ {t - p} + \sigma^ {(s _ {t})} \varepsilon_ {t}\tag{4.112}
$$

<sup>24</sup>Mixtures of finitely many normals, each with different means and variances, can be used approximate many nonnormal distributions.

In each panel, the large subpanel contains the generated data, the top right subpanel contains a kernel density estimate of the unconditional density and the bottom right subpanel contains the time series of the state values (high points correspond to the high state).


Let $- \infty = Y _ { 0 } < Y _ { 1 } < Y _ { 2 } < . . . < Y _ { N } < Y _ { N + 1 } = \infty$ be a partition of $y$ in to $N + 1$ distinct bins. $s _ { t } = j$ is $Y _ { t - k } \in ( Y _ { j } , Y _ { j + 1 } )$ 

The primary application of SETAR models in finance has been to exchange rates which often exhibit a behavior that is difficult to model with standard ARMA models: many FX rates exhibit random-walk-like behavior in a range yet remain within the band longer than would be consistent with a simple random walk. A symmetric SETAR is a parsimonious model that can describe this behavior and is parameterized 

$$
\begin{array}{c} Y _ {t} = Y _ {t - 1} + \varepsilon_ {t} \text {   if   } C - \delta <   Y _ {t} <   C + \delta \\ Y _ {t} = C (1 - \phi) + \phi Y _ {t - 1} + \varepsilon_ {t} \text {   if   } Y _ {t} <   C - \delta \text {   or   } Y _ {t} > C + \delta \end{array}\tag{4.113}
$$

where $C$ is the “target” exchange rate. The first equation is a standard random walk, and when $Y _ { t }$ is within the target band, it behaves like a random walk. The second equation is only relevant when $Y _ { t }$ is outside of its target band and ensures that $Y _ { t }$ is mean-reverting towards $C$ as long as $\vert \phi \vert < 1 . ^ { 2 6 } \ \phi$ is usually assumed to lie between 0 and 1 which produces a smooth mean reversion back towards the band. 

To illustrate this process’s behavior and highlight the differences between it and a random walk, 200 data points were generated with different values of $\phi$ using standard normal innovations. The mean was set to 100 and the used $\delta = 5$ , and so $Y _ { t }$ follows a random walk when between 95 and 105. The lag value of the threshold variable (k) was set to one. Four values for $\phi$ were used: 0, 0.5, 0.9 and 1. The extreme cases represent a process which is immediately mean-reverting $( \phi = 0 )$ , in which case as soon as $Y _ { t }$ leaves the target band it is immediately returned to $C ,$ and a process that is a pure random walk $( \phi = 1 )$ since $Y _ { t } = Y _ { t - 1 } + \varepsilon _ { t }$ for any value of $Y _ { t - 1 }$ . The two interior cases represent smooth reversion back to the band; when $\phi = . 5$ , the reversion is quick, and when $\phi = . 9$ the reversion is slow. When $\phi$ is close to 1, it is challenging to differentiate a band SETAR from a pure random walk, which is one of the explanations for the poor performance of unit root tests where tests often fail to reject a unit root despite clear economic theory predicting that a time series should be mean reverting. 

## 4.A Computing Autocovariance and Autocorrelations

This appendix covers the derivation of the ACF for the MA(1), MA(Q), AR(1), AR(2), AR(3), and $\mathbf { A R M A } ( 1 , 1 )$ . Throughout this appendix, $\left\{ \varepsilon _ { t } \right\}$ is assumed to be a white noise process, and the processes parameters are always assumed to be consistent with covariance stationarity. All models are assumed to be mean $0 ,$ an assumption made without loss of generality since autocovariances are defined using demeaned time series, 

$$
\gamma_ {s} = \mathrm{E} [ (Y _ {t} - \mu) (Y _ {t - s} - \mu) ]
$$

where $\mu = \operatorname { E } [ Y _ { t } ]$ . Recall that the autocorrelation is simply the of the $\mathrm { s } ^ { \mathrm { t h } }$ autocovariance to the variance, 

$$
\rho_ {s} = \frac {\gamma_ {s}}{\gamma_ {0}}.
$$

This appendix presents two methods for deriving the autocorrelations of ARMA processes: backward substitution and the Yule-Walker equations, a set of k equations with $k$ unknowns where $\gamma _ { 0 } , \gamma _ { 1 } , \ldots , \gamma _ { k - 1 }$ are the solution. 

## 4.A.1 Yule-Walker

The Yule-Walker equations are a linear system of max $( P , Q ) + 1$ equations (in an ARMA(P, Q)) where the solution to the system is the long-run variance and the first k 1 autocovariances. The Yule-Walker 

<sup>26</sup>Recall the mean of an AR(1) $Y _ { t } = \phi _ { 0 } + \phi _ { 1 } Y _ { t - 1 } + \varepsilon _ { t } { \mathrm { ~ i s ~ } } \phi _ { 0 } / ( 1 - \phi _ { 1 } )$ where $\phi _ { 0 } = C \big ( 1 - \phi \big )$ and $\phi _ { 1 } = \phi$ in this SETAR. 

Self Exciting Threshold Autoregression Processes 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/2f781a94-c477-46c8-9e23-a51a2f84adec/31ab6ae31fe7933089145f0b2a8240956e44ac2de93f034be6fbe6b10739c501.jpg)



Figure 4.14: The four panels of this figure contain simulated data generated by a SETAR with different values of $\phi$ . When $\phi = 0$ the process is immediately returned to its unconditional mean $C = 1 0 0$ Larger values of $\phi$ increase the amount of time spent outside of the “target band” (95–105) and when $\phi = 1$ , the process is a pure random walk.


equations are formed by equating the definition of an autocovariance with an expansion produced by substituting for the contemporaneous value of $Y _ { t } .$ . For example, suppose $Y _ { t }$ follows an AR(2) process, 

$$
Y _ {t} = \phi_ {1} Y _ {t - 1} + \phi_ {2} Y _ {t - 2} + \varepsilon_ {t}
$$

The variance must satisfy 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\operatorname{E} [ Y _ {t} Y _ {t} ] = \operatorname{E} [ Y _ {t} (\phi_ {1} Y _ {t - 1} + \phi_ {2} Y _ {t - 2} + \varepsilon_ {t}) ]} \\ & {\operatorname{E} [ Y _ {t} ^ {2} ] = \operatorname{E} [ \phi_ {1} Y _ {t} Y _ {t - 1} + \phi_ {2} Y _ {t} Y _ {t - 2} + Y _ {t} \varepsilon_ {t} ]} \\ & {\operatorname{V} [ Y _ {t} ] = \phi_ {1} \operatorname{E} [ Y _ {t} Y _ {t - 1} ] + \phi_ {2} \operatorname{E} [ Y _ {t} Y _ {t - 2} ] + \operatorname{E} [ Y _ {t} \varepsilon_ {t} ].} \end{array}\tag{4.114}
$$

In the final equation above, terms of the form E $\left[ Y _ { t } Y _ { t - s } \right]$ are replaced by their population values, $\gamma _ { s }$ and $\mathrm { E } [ Y _ { t } \varepsilon _ { t } ]$ is replaced with its population value, $\sigma ^ { 2 }$ 

$$
\mathbf {V} [ Y _ {t} Y _ {t} ] = \phi_ {1} \mathrm{E} [ Y _ {t} Y _ {t - 1} ] + \phi_ {2} \mathrm{E} [ Y _ {t} Y _ {t - 2} ] + \mathrm{E} [ Y _ {t} \pmb {\varepsilon} _ {t} ]\tag{4.115}
$$

becomes 

$$
\gamma_ {0} = \phi_ {1} \gamma_ {1} + \phi_ {2} \gamma_ {2} + \sigma^ {2}\tag{4.116}
$$

and so the long run variance is a function of the first two autocovariances, the model parameters, and the innovation variance. This can be repeated for the first autocovariance, 

$$
\operatorname{E} [ Y _ {t} Y _ {t - 1} ] = \phi_ {1} \operatorname{E} [ Y _ {t - 1} Y _ {t - 1} ] + \phi_ {2} \operatorname{E} [ Y _ {t - 1} Y _ {t - 2} ] + \operatorname{E} [ Y _ {t - 1} \pmb {\varepsilon} _ {t} ]
$$

becomes 

$$
\gamma_ {1} = \phi_ {1} \gamma_ {0} + \phi_ {2} \gamma_ {1},\tag{4.117}
$$

and for the second autocovariance, 

$$
\mathrm{E} \left[ Y _ {t} Y _ {t - 2} \right] = \phi_ {1} \mathrm{E} \left[ Y _ {t - 2} Y _ {t - 1} \right] + \phi_ {2} \mathrm{E} \left[ Y _ {t - 2} Y _ {t - 2} \right] + \mathrm{E} \left[ Y _ {t - 2} \varepsilon_ {t} \right] \text {   becomes   }
$$

becomes 

$$
\gamma_ {2} = \phi_ {1} \gamma_ {1} + \phi_ {2} \gamma_ {0}.\tag{4.118}
$$

Together eqs. (4.116), (4.117) and (4.118) form a system of three equations with three unknowns. The Yule-Walker method relies heavily on the covariance stationarity and so $\operatorname { E } [ Y _ { t } Y _ { t - j } ] = E [ Y _ { t - h } Y _ { t - h - j } ]$ for any h. This property of covariance stationary processes was repeatedly used in forming the producing the Yule-Walker equations since $\operatorname { E } [ Y _ { t } Y _ { t } ] = \operatorname { E } [ Y _ { t - 1 } Y _ { t - 1 } ] = \operatorname { E } [ Y _ { t - 2 } Y _ { t - 2 } ] = \gamma _ { 0 }$ and $\operatorname { E } [ Y _ { t } Y _ { t - 1 } ] =$ $\operatorname { E } [ Y _ { t - 1 } Y _ { t - 2 } ] = \gamma _ { 1 }$ .The Yule-Walker method will be demonstrated for several models, starting from a simple MA(1) and working up to an ARMA(1,1). 

## 4.A.1.1 MA(1)

The autocorrelations of the MA(1) are simple to derive. 

$$
Y _ {t} = \theta_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 1} + \varepsilon_ {t}
$$

The Yule-Walker equations are 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \operatorname{E} [ Y _ {t} Y _ {t} ] = \operatorname{E} [ \theta_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 1} Y _ {t} ] + \operatorname{E} [ \varepsilon_ {t} Y _ {t} ] \\ \operatorname{E} [ Y _ {t} Y _ {t - 1} ] = \operatorname{E} [ \theta_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 1} Y _ {t - 1} ] + \operatorname{E} [ \varepsilon_ {t} Y _ {t - 1} ] \\ \operatorname{E} [ Y _ {t} Y _ {t - 2} ] = \operatorname{E} [ \theta_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 1} Y _ {t - 2} ] + \operatorname{E} [ \varepsilon_ {t} Y _ {t - 2} ] \end{array}\tag{4.119}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{l} \gamma_ {0} = \theta_ {1} ^ {2} \sigma^ {2} + \sigma^ {2} \\ \gamma_ {1} = \theta_ {1} \sigma^ {2} \\ \gamma_ {2} = 0 \end{array}\tag{4.120}
$$

Additionally, both $\gamma _ { s }$ and $\rho _ { s } , s \ge 2$ are 0 by the white noise property of the residuals, and so the autocorrelations are 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \rho_ {1} = \frac {\theta_ {1} \sigma^ {2}}{\theta_ {1} ^ {2} \sigma^ {2} + \sigma^ {2}} \\ = \frac {\theta_ {1}}{1 + \theta_ {1} ^ {2}}, \\ \rho_ {2} = 0. \end{array}
$$

## 4.A.1.2 MA(Q)

The Yule-Walker equations can be constructed and solved for any $\mathbf { M A } ( Q )$ , and the structure of the autocovariance is simple to detect by constructing a subset of the full system. 

(4.121) 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\mathrm{E} [ Y _ {t} Y _ {t} ] = \mathrm{E} [ \theta_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 1} Y _ {t} ] + \mathrm{E} [ \theta_ {2} \varepsilon_ {t - 2} Y _ {t} ] + \mathrm{E} [ \theta_ {3} \varepsilon_ {t - 3} Y _ {t} ] + \ldots + \mathrm{E} [ \theta_ {Q} \varepsilon_ {t - Q} Y _ {t} ]} \\ & {\quad \gamma_ {0} = \theta_ {1} ^ {2} \sigma^ {2} + \theta_ {2} ^ {2} \sigma^ {2} + \theta_ {3} ^ {2} \sigma^ {2} + \ldots + \theta_ {Q} ^ {2} \sigma^ {2} + \sigma^ {2}} \\ & {\qquad = \sigma^ {2} (1 + \theta_ {1} ^ {2} + \theta_ {2} ^ {2} + \theta_ {3} ^ {2} + \ldots + \theta_ {Q} ^ {2})} \\ & {\mathrm{E} [ Y _ {t} Y _ {t - 1} ] = \mathrm{E} [ \theta_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 1} Y _ {t - 1} ] + \mathrm{E} [ \theta_ {2} \varepsilon_ {t - 2} Y _ {t - 1} ] + \mathrm{E} [ \theta_ {3} \varepsilon_ {t - 3} Y _ {t - 1} ] + \ldots + \mathrm{E} [ \theta_ {Q} \varepsilon_ {t - Q} Y _ {t - 1} ]} \\ & {\quad \gamma_ {1} = \theta_ {1} \sigma^ {2} + \theta_ {1} \theta_ {2} \sigma^ {2} + \theta_ {2} \theta_ {3} \sigma^ {2} + \ldots + \theta_ {Q - 1} \theta_ {Q} \sigma^ {2}} \\ & {\qquad = \sigma^ {2} (\theta_ {1} + \theta_ {1} \theta_ {2} + \theta_ {2} \theta_ {3} + \ldots + \theta_ {Q - 1} \theta_ {Q})} \\ & {\mathrm{E} [ Y _ {t} Y _ {t - 2} ] = \mathrm{E} [ \theta_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 1} Y _ {t - 2} ] + \mathrm{E} [ \theta_ {2} \varepsilon_ {t - 2} Y _ {t - 2} ] + \mathrm{E} [ \theta_ {3} \varepsilon_ {t - 3} Y _ {t - 2} ] + \ldots + \mathrm{E} [ \theta_ {Q} \varepsilon_ {t - Q} Y _ {t - 2} ]} \\ & {\quad \gamma_ {2} = \theta_ {2} \sigma^ {2} + \theta_ {1} \theta_ {3} \sigma^ {2} + \theta_ {2} \theta_ {4} \sigma^ {2} + \ldots + \theta_ {Q - 2} \theta_ {Q} \sigma^ {2}} \\ & {\qquad = \sigma^ {2} (\theta_ {2} + \theta_ {1} \theta_ {3} + \theta_ {2} \theta_ {4} + \ldots + \theta_ {Q - 2} \theta_ {Q})} \end{array}\tag{4.122}
$$

(4.123) 

The pattern that emerges shows, 

$$
\gamma_ {s} = \theta_ {s} \sigma^ {2} + \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {Q - s} \sigma^ {2} \theta_ {i} \theta_ {i + s} = \sigma^ {2} (\theta_ {s} + \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {Q - s} \theta_ {i} \theta_ {i + s}).
$$

and $\mathbf { S O }$ , $\gamma _ { s }$ is a sum of $Q - s + 1$ terms. The autocorrelations are 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \rho_ {1} = \frac {\theta_ {1} + \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {Q - 1} \theta_ {i} \theta_ {i + 1}}{1 + \theta_ {s} + \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {Q} \theta_ {i} ^ {2}} \\ \rho_ {2} = \frac {\theta_ {2} + \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {Q - 2} \theta_ {i} \theta_ {i + 2}}{1 + \theta_ {s} + \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {Q} \theta_ {i} ^ {2}} \\ \vdots = \qquad \vdots \\ \rho_ {Q} = \frac {\theta_ {Q}}{1 + \theta_ {s} + \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {Q} \theta_ {i} ^ {2}} \\ \rho_ {Q + s} = 0, \quad s \geq 0 \end{array}\tag{4.124}
$$

4.A.1.3 AR(1) 

The Yule-Walker method requires be max $( P , Q ) + 1$ equations to compute the autocovariance for an $\mathbf { A R M A } ( P , Q )$ process and in an $\mathrm { A R } ( 1 )$ , two are required (the third is included to establish this point). 

$$
Y _ {t} = \phi_ {1} Y _ {t - 1} + \varepsilon_ {t}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{c} \operatorname{E} [ Y _ {t} Y _ {t} ] = \operatorname{E} [ \phi_ {1} Y _ {t - 1} Y _ {t} ] + \operatorname{E} [ \varepsilon_ {t} Y _ {t} ] \\ \operatorname{E} [ Y _ {t} Y _ {t - 1} ] = \operatorname{E} [ \phi_ {1} Y _ {t - 1} Y _ {t - 1} ] + \operatorname{E} [ \varepsilon_ {t} Y _ {t - 1} ] \\ \operatorname{E} [ Y _ {t} Y _ {t - 2} ] = \operatorname{E} [ \phi_ {1} Y _ {t - 1} Y _ {t - 2} ] + \operatorname{E} [ \varepsilon_ {t} Y _ {t - 2} ] \end{array}\tag{4.125}
$$

These equations can be rewritten in terms of the autocovariances, model parameters and $\sigma ^ { 2 }$ by taking expectation and noting that $\operatorname { E } [ \varepsilon _ { t } Y _ { t } ] = \sigma ^ { 2 }$ since $Y _ { t } = \pmb { \varepsilon } _ { t } + \phi _ { 1 } \pmb { \varepsilon } _ { t - 1 } + \phi _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } \pmb { \varepsilon } _ { t - 2 } + . .$ . and $\operatorname { E } [ \varepsilon _ { t } Y _ { t - j } ] = 0 , j > 0$ since $\left\{ \varepsilon _ { t } \right\}$ is a white noise process. 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \gamma_ {0} = \phi_ {1} \gamma_ {1} + \sigma^ {2} \\ \gamma_ {1} = \phi_ {1} \gamma_ {0} \\ \gamma_ {2} = \phi_ {1} \gamma_ {1} \end{array}\tag{4.126}
$$

The third is redundant since $\gamma _ { 2 }$ is fully determined by $\gamma _ { 1 }$ and $\phi _ { 1 }$ , and higher autocovariances are similarly redundant since $\gamma _ { s } = \phi _ { 1 } \gamma _ { s - 1 }$ for any $s .$ The first two equations can be solved for $\%$ and $\gamma _ { 1 }$ , 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \gamma_ {0} & = & \phi_ {1} \gamma_ {1} + \sigma^ {2} \\ \gamma_ {1} & = & \phi_ {1} \gamma_ {0} \\ \Rightarrow \gamma_ {0} & = & \phi_ {1} ^ {2} \gamma_ {0} + \sigma^ {2} \\ \Rightarrow \gamma_ {0} - \phi_ {1} ^ {2} \gamma_ {0} & = & \sigma^ {2} \\ \Rightarrow \gamma_ {0} (1 - \phi_ {1} ^ {2}) & = & \sigma^ {2} \\ \Rightarrow \gamma_ {0} & = & \frac {\sigma^ {2}}{1 - \phi_ {1} ^ {2}} \end{array}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{array}{r c l} \gamma_ {1} & = & \phi_ {1} \gamma_ {0} \\ \gamma_ {0} & = & \frac {\sigma^ {2}}{1 - \phi_ {1} ^ {2}} \\ \Rightarrow \gamma_ {1} & = & \phi_ {1} \frac {\sigma^ {2}}{1 - \phi_ {1} ^ {2}}. \end{array}
$$

The remaining autocovariances can be computed using the recursion $\gamma _ { s } = \phi _ { 1 } \gamma _ { s - 1 }$ , and so 

$$
\gamma_ {s} = \phi_ {1} ^ {2} \frac {\sigma^ {2}}{1 - \phi_ {1} ^ {2}}.
$$

Finally, the autocorrelations can be computed as ratios of autocovariances, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \rho_ {1} = \frac {\gamma_ {1}}{\gamma_ {0}} = \phi_ {1} \frac {\sigma^ {s}}{1 - \phi_ {1} ^ {2}} \bigg / \frac {\sigma^ {2}}{1 - \phi_ {1} ^ {2}} \\ \rho_ {1} = \phi_ {1} \end{array}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{l} \rho_ {s} = \frac {\gamma_ {s}}{\gamma_ {0}} = \phi_ {1} ^ {s} \frac {\sigma^ {2}}{1 - \phi_ {1} ^ {2}} \Big / \frac {\sigma^ {2}}{1 - \phi_ {1} ^ {2}} \\ \rho_ {s} = \phi_ {1} ^ {s}. \end{array}
$$

## 4.A.1.4 AR(2)

The autocorrelations in an $\operatorname { A R } ( 2 )$ 

$$
Y _ {t} = \phi_ {1} Y _ {t - 1} + \phi_ {2} Y _ {t - 2} + \varepsilon_ {t}
$$

can be similarly computed using the max $( P , Q ) + 1$ equation Yule-Walker system, 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \operatorname{E} [ Y _ {t} Y _ {t} ] = \phi_ {1} \operatorname{E} [ Y _ {t - 1} Y _ {t} ] + \phi_ {2} \operatorname{E} [ Y _ {t - 2} Y _ {t} ] + \operatorname{E} \varepsilon_ {t} Y _ {t} ] \\ \operatorname{E} [ Y _ {t} Y _ {t - 1} ] = \phi_ {1} \operatorname{E} [ Y _ {t - 1} Y _ {t - 1} ] + \phi_ {2} \operatorname{E} [ Y _ {t - 2} Y _ {t - 1} ] + \operatorname{E} [ \varepsilon_ {t} Y _ {t - 1} ] \\ \operatorname{E} [ Y _ {t} Y _ {t - 2} ] = \phi_ {1} \operatorname{E} [ Y _ {t - 1} Y _ {t - 2} ] + \phi_ {2} \operatorname{E} [ Y _ {t - 2} Y _ {t - 2} ] + \operatorname{E} [ \varepsilon_ {t} Y _ {t - 2} ] \end{array}\tag{4.127}
$$

and then replacing expectations with their population counterparts, γ<sub>0</sub>,γ<sub>1</sub>, $\gamma _ { 2 }$ and $\sigma ^ { 2 }$ . 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \gamma_ {0} = \phi_ {1} \gamma_ {1} + \phi_ {2} \gamma_ {2} + \sigma^ {2} \\ \gamma_ {1} = \phi_ {1} \gamma_ {0} + \phi_ {2} \gamma_ {1} \\ \gamma_ {2} = \phi_ {1} \gamma_ {1} + \phi_ {2} \gamma_ {0} \end{array}\tag{4.128}
$$

Further, it must be the case that $\gamma _ { s } = \phi _ { 1 } \gamma _ { s - 1 } + \phi _ { 2 } \gamma _ { s - 2 }$ for $s \geq 2$ . To solve this system of equations, divide the autocovariance equations by $\gamma _ { 0 } .$ , the long run variance. Omitting the first equation, the system reduces to two equations in two unknowns, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \rho_ {1} = \phi_ {1} \rho_ {0} + \phi_ {2} \rho_ {1} \\ \rho_ {2} = \phi_ {1} \rho_ {1} + \phi_ {2} \rho_ {0} \end{array}
$$

since $\rho _ { 0 } = \gamma _ { 0 } / \gamma _ { 0 } = 1$ 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \rho_ {1} = \phi_ {1} + \phi_ {2} \rho_ {1} \\ \rho_ {2} = \phi_ {1} \rho_ {1} + \phi_ {2} \end{array}
$$

Solving this system, 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \rho_ {1} = \phi_ {1} + \phi_ {2} \rho_ {1} \\ \rho_ {1} - \phi_ {2} \rho_ {1} = \phi_ {1} \\ \rho_ {1} (1 - \phi_ {2}) = \phi_ {1} \\ \rho_ {1} = \frac {\phi_ {1}}{1 - \phi_ {2}} \end{array}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \rho_ {2} & = \phi_ {1} \rho_ {1} + \phi_ {2} \\ & = \phi_ {1} \frac {\phi_ {1}}{1 - \phi_ {2}} + \phi_ {2} \\ & = \frac {\phi_ {1} \phi_ {1} + (1 - \phi_ {2}) \phi_ {2}}{1 - \phi_ {2}} \\ & = \frac {\phi_ {1} ^ {2} + \phi_ {2} - \phi_ {2} ^ {2}}{1 - \phi_ {2}} \end{array}
$$

Since $\rho _ { s } = \phi _ { 1 } \rho _ { s - 1 } + \phi _ { 2 } \rho _ { s - 2 }$ , these first two autocorrelations are sufficient to compute the other autocorrelations, 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \rho_ {3} & = \phi_ {1} \rho_ {2} + \phi_ {2} \rho_ {1} \\ & = \phi_ {1} \frac {\phi_ {1} ^ {2} + \phi_ {2} - \phi_ {2} ^ {2}}{1 - \phi_ {2}} + \phi_ {2} \frac {\phi_ {1}}{1 - \phi_ {2}} \end{array}
$$

and the long run variance of $Y _ { t }$ , 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \gamma_ {0} = \phi_ {1} \gamma_ {1} + \phi_ {2} \gamma_ {2} + \sigma^ {2} \\ \gamma_ {0} - \phi_ {1} \gamma_ {1} - \phi_ {2} \gamma_ {2} = \sigma^ {2} \\ \gamma_ {0} (1 - \phi_ {1} \rho_ {1} - \phi_ {2} \rho_ {2}) = \sigma^ {2} \\ \gamma_ {0} = \frac {\sigma^ {2}}{1 - \phi_ {1} \rho_ {1} - \phi_ {2} \rho_ {2}} \end{array}
$$

The final solution is computed by substituting for $\rho _ { 1 }$ and $\rho _ { 2 }$ , 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \gamma_ {0} = \frac {\sigma^ {2}}{1 - \phi_ {1} \frac {\phi_ {1}}{1 - \phi_ {2}} - \phi_ {2} \frac {\phi_ {1} ^ {2} + \phi_ {2} - \phi_ {2} ^ {2}}{1 - \phi_ {2}}} \\ = \frac {1 - \phi_ {2}}{1 + \phi_ {2}} \left(\frac {\sigma^ {2}}{(\phi_ {1} + \phi_ {2} - 1) (\phi_ {2} - \phi_ {1} - 1)}\right) \end{array}
$$

## 4.A.1.5 AR(3)

Begin by constructing the Yule-Walker equations, 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \mathrm{E} [ Y _ {t} Y _ {t} ] = \phi_ {1} \mathrm{E} [ Y _ {t - 1} Y _ {t} ] + \phi_ {2} \mathrm{E} [ Y _ {t - 2} Y _ {t} ] + \phi_ {3} \mathrm{E} [ Y _ {t - 3} Y _ {t} ] + \mathrm{E} [ \varepsilon_ {t} Y _ {t} ] \\ \mathrm{E} [ Y _ {t} Y _ {t - 1} ] = \phi_ {1} \mathrm{E} [ Y _ {t - 1} Y _ {t - 1} ] + \phi_ {2} \mathrm{E} [ Y _ {t - 2} Y _ {t - 1} ] + \phi_ {3} \mathrm{E} [ Y _ {t - 3} Y _ {t - 1} ] + \mathrm{E} [ \varepsilon_ {t} Y _ {t - 1} ] \\ \mathrm{E} [ Y _ {t} Y _ {t - 2} ] = \phi_ {1} \mathrm{E} [ Y _ {t - 1} Y _ {t - 2} ] + \phi_ {2} \mathrm{E} [ Y _ {t - 2} Y _ {t - 2} ] + \phi_ {3} \mathrm{E} [ Y _ {t - 3} Y _ {t - 2} ] + \mathrm{E} [ \varepsilon_ {t} Y _ {t - 2} ] \\ \mathrm{E} [ Y _ {t} Y _ {t - 3} ] = \phi_ {1} \mathrm{E} [ Y _ {t - 1} Y _ {t - 3} ] + \phi_ {2} \mathrm{E} [ Y _ {t - 2} Y _ {t - 3} ] + \phi_ {3} \mathrm{E} [ Y _ {t - 3} Y _ {t - 3} ] + \mathrm{E} [ \varepsilon_ {t} Y _ {t - 4} ]. \end{array}
$$

Replacing the expectations with their population values, $\gamma _ { 0 } , \gamma _ { 1 } , \ldots$ . and $\sigma ^ { 2 }$ , the Yule-Walker equations can be rewritten 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \gamma_ {0} = \phi_ {1} \gamma_ {1} + \phi_ {2} \gamma_ {2} + \phi_ {3} \gamma_ {3} + \sigma^ {2} \\ \gamma_ {1} = \phi_ {1} \gamma_ {0} + \phi_ {2} \gamma_ {1} + \phi_ {3} \gamma_ {2} \\ \gamma_ {2} = \phi_ {1} \gamma_ {1} + \phi_ {2} \gamma_ {0} + \phi_ {3} \gamma_ {1} \\ \gamma_ {3} = \phi_ {1} \gamma_ {2} + \phi_ {2} \gamma_ {1} + \phi_ {3} \gamma_ {0} \end{array}\tag{4.129}
$$

and the recursive relationship $\gamma _ { s } = \phi _ { 1 } \gamma _ { s - 1 } + \phi _ { 2 } \gamma _ { s - 2 } + \phi _ { 3 } \gamma _ { s - 3 }$ can be observed for $s \geq 3$ .Omitting the first condition and dividing by $\gamma _ { 0 } .$ , 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \rho_ {1} = \phi_ {1} \rho_ {0} + \phi_ {2} \rho_ {1} + \phi_ {3} \rho_ {2} \\ \rho_ {2} = \phi_ {1} \rho_ {1} + \phi_ {2} \rho_ {0} + \phi_ {3} \rho_ {1} \\ \rho_ {3} = \phi_ {1} \rho_ {2} + \phi_ {2} \rho_ {1} + \phi_ {3} \rho_ {0}. \end{array}
$$

leaving three equations in three unknowns since $\rho _ { 0 } = \gamma _ { 0 } / \gamma _ { 0 } = 1$ 

$$
\rho_ {1} = \phi_ {1} + \phi_ {2} \rho_ {1} + \phi_ {3} \rho_ {2}
$$

$$
\rho_ {2} = \phi_ {1} \rho_ {1} + \phi_ {2} + \phi_ {3} \rho_ {1}
$$

$$
\rho_ {3} = \phi_ {1} \rho_ {2} + \phi_ {2} \rho_ {1} + \phi_ {3}
$$

Following some tedious algebra, the solution to this system is 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \rho_ {1} = \frac {\phi_ {1} + \phi_ {2} \phi_ {3}}{1 - \phi_ {2} - \phi_ {1} \phi_ {3} - \phi_ {3} ^ {2}} \\ \rho_ {2} = \frac {\phi_ {2} + \phi_ {1} ^ {2} + \phi_ {3} \phi_ {1} - \phi_ {2} ^ {2}}{1 - \phi_ {2} - \phi_ {1} \phi_ {3} - \phi_ {3} ^ {2}} \\ \rho_ {3} = \frac {\phi_ {3} + \phi_ {1} ^ {3} + \phi_ {1} ^ {2} \phi_ {3} + \phi_ {1} \phi_ {2} ^ {2} + 2 \phi_ {1} \phi_ {2} + \phi_ {2} ^ {2} \phi_ {3} - \phi_ {2} \phi_ {3} - \phi_ {1} \phi_ {3} ^ {2} - \phi_ {3} ^ {3}}{1 - \phi_ {2} - \phi_ {1} \phi_ {3} - \phi_ {3} ^ {2}}. \end{array}
$$

Finally, the unconditional variance can be computed using the first three autocorrelations, 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \gamma_ {0} = \phi_ {1} \gamma_ {1} + \phi_ {2} \gamma_ {2} + \phi_ {3} \gamma_ {3} \sigma^ {2} \\ \gamma_ {0} - \phi_ {1} \gamma_ {1} - \phi_ {2} \gamma_ {2} - \phi_ {3} \gamma_ {3} = \sigma^ {2} \\ \gamma_ {0} (1 - \phi_ {1} \rho_ {1} + \phi_ {2} \rho_ {2} + \phi_ {3} \rho_ {3}) = \sigma^ {2} \\ \gamma_ {0} = \frac {\sigma^ {2}}{1 - \phi_ {1} \rho_ {1} - \phi_ {2} \rho_ {2} - \phi_ {3} \rho_ {3}} \\ \gamma_ {0} = \frac {\sigma^ {2} (1 - \phi_ {2} - \phi_ {1} \phi_ {3} - \phi_ {3} ^ {2})}{(1 - \phi_ {2} - \phi_ {3} - \phi_ {1}) (1 + \phi_ {2} + \phi_ {3} \phi_ {1} - \phi_ {3} ^ {2}) (1 + \phi_ {3} + \phi_ {1} - \phi_ {2})} \end{array}
$$

## 4.A.1.6 ARMA(1,1)

Deriving the autocovariances and autocorrelations of an ARMA process is more complicated than for a pure AR or MA process. An ARMA(1,1) is specified as 

$$
Y _ {t} = \phi_ {1} Y _ {t - 1} + \theta_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 1} + \varepsilon_ {t}
$$

and since $P = Q = 1$ , the Yule-Walker system requires two equations, noting that the third or higher autocovariance is a trivial function of the first two autocovariances. 

$$
\begin{array}{r} \mathrm{E} [ Y _ {t} Y _ {t} ] = \mathrm{E} [ \phi_ {1} Y _ {t - 1} Y _ {t} ] + \mathrm{E} [ \theta_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 1} Y _ {t} ] + \mathrm{E} [ \varepsilon_ {t} Y _ {t} ] \\ \mathrm{E} [ Y _ {t} Y _ {t - 1} ] = \mathrm{E} [ \phi_ {1} Y _ {t - 1} Y _ {t - 1} ] + \mathrm{E} [ \theta_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 1} Y _ {t - 1} ] + \mathrm{E} [ \varepsilon_ {t} Y _ {t - 1} ] \end{array}\tag{4.130}
$$

The presence of the $\operatorname { E } [ \theta _ { 1 } \varepsilon _ { t - 1 } Y _ { t } ]$ term in the first equation complicates solving this system since $\varepsilon _ { t - 1 }$ appears in $Y _ { t }$ directly though $\theta _ { 1 } \varepsilon _ { t - 1 }$ and indirectly through $\phi _ { 1 } Y _ { t - 1 }$ . The non-zero relationships can be determined by recursively substituting $Y _ { t }$ until it consists of only $\varepsilon _ { t } , \varepsilon _ { t - 1 }$ and $Y _ { t - 2 }$ (since $Y _ { t - 2 }$ is uncorrelated with $\varepsilon _ { t - 1 }$ by the WN assumption). 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} Y _ {t} & = \phi_ {1} Y _ {t - 1} + \theta_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 1} + \varepsilon_ {t} \\ & = \phi_ {1} (\phi_ {1} Y _ {t - 2} + \theta_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 2} + \varepsilon_ {t - 1}) + \theta_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 1} + \varepsilon_ {t} \\ & = \phi_ {1} ^ {2} Y _ {t - 2} + \phi_ {1} \theta_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 2} + \phi_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 1} + \theta_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 1} + \varepsilon_ {t} \\ & = \phi_ {1} ^ {2} Y _ {t - 2} + \phi_ {1} \theta_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 2} + (\phi_ {1} + \theta_ {1}) \varepsilon_ {t - 1} + \varepsilon_ {t} \end{array}\tag{4.131}
$$

and so $\operatorname { E } [ \theta _ { 1 } \varepsilon _ { t - 1 } Y _ { t } ] = \theta _ { 1 } ( \phi _ { 1 } + \theta _ { 1 } ) \sigma ^ { 2 }$ and the Yule-Walker equations can be expressed using the population moments and model parameters. 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \gamma_ {0} = \phi_ {1} \gamma_ {1} + \theta_ {1} (\phi_ {1} + \theta_ {1}) \sigma^ {2} + \sigma^ {2} \\ \gamma_ {1} = \phi_ {1} \gamma_ {0} + \theta_ {1} \sigma^ {2} \end{array}
$$

These two equations in two unknowns which can be solved, 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \gamma_ {0} & = \phi_ {1} \gamma_ {1} + \theta_ {1} (\phi_ {1} + \theta_ {1}) \sigma^ {2} + \sigma^ {2} \\ & = \phi_ {1} (\phi_ {1} \gamma_ {0} + \theta_ {1} \sigma^ {2}) + \theta_ {1} (\phi_ {1} + \theta_ {1}) \sigma^ {2} + \sigma^ {2} \\ & = \phi_ {1} ^ {2} \gamma_ {0} + \phi_ {1} \theta_ {1} \sigma^ {2} + \theta_ {1} (\phi_ {1} + \theta_ {1}) \sigma^ {2} + \sigma^ {2} \\ \gamma_ {0} - \phi_ {1} ^ {2} \gamma_ {0} & = \sigma^ {2} (\phi_ {1} \theta_ {1} + \phi_ {1} \theta_ {1} + \theta_ {1} ^ {2} + 1) \\ \gamma_ {0} & = \frac {\sigma^ {2} (1 + \theta_ {1} ^ {2} + 2 \phi_ {1} \theta_ {1})}{1 - \phi_ {1} ^ {2}} \end{array}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{l} \gamma_ {1} = \phi_ {1} \gamma_ {0} + \theta_ {1} \sigma^ {2} \\ = \phi_ {1} \left(\frac {\sigma^ {2} (1 + \theta_ {1} ^ {2} + 2 \phi_ {1} \theta_ {1})}{1 - \phi_ {1} ^ {2}}\right) + \theta_ {1} \sigma^ {2} \\ = \phi_ {1} \left(\frac {\sigma^ {2} (1 + \theta_ {1} ^ {2} + 2 \phi_ {1} \theta_ {1})}{1 - \phi_ {1} ^ {2}}\right) + \frac {(1 - \phi_ {1} ^ {2}) \theta_ {1} \sigma^ {2}}{1 - \phi_ {1} ^ {2}} \\ = \frac {\sigma^ {2} (\phi_ {1} + \phi_ {1} \theta_ {1} ^ {2} + 2 \phi_ {1} ^ {2} \theta_ {1})}{1 - \phi_ {1} ^ {2}} + \frac {(\theta_ {1} - \theta_ {1} \phi_ {1} ^ {2}) \sigma^ {2}}{1 - \phi_ {1} ^ {2}} \\ = \frac {\sigma^ {2} (\phi_ {1} + \phi_ {1} \theta_ {1} ^ {2} + 2 \phi_ {1} ^ {2} \theta_ {1} + \theta_ {1} - \phi_ {1} ^ {2} \theta_ {1})}{1 - \phi_ {1} ^ {2}} \\ = \frac {\sigma^ {2} (\phi_ {1} ^ {2} \theta_ {1} + \phi_ {1} \theta_ {1} ^ {2} + \phi_ {1} + \theta_ {1})}{1 - \phi_ {1} ^ {2}} \\ = \frac {\sigma^ {2} (\phi_ {1} + \theta_ {1}) (\phi_ {1} \theta_ {1} + 1)}{1 - \phi_ {1} ^ {2}} \end{array}
$$

and so the $1 ^ { \mathrm { s t } }$ autocorrelation is 

$$
\rho_ {1} = \frac {\frac {\sigma^ {2} (\phi_ {1} + \theta_ {1}) (\phi_ {1} \theta_ {1} + 1)}{1 - \phi_ {1} ^ {2}}}{\frac {\sigma^ {2} (1 + \theta_ {1} ^ {2} + 2 \phi_ {1} \theta_ {1})}{1 - \phi_ {1} ^ {2}}} = \frac {(\phi_ {1} + \theta_ {1}) (\phi_ {1} \theta_ {1} + 1)}{(1 + \theta_ {1} ^ {2} + 2 \phi_ {1} \theta_ {1})}.
$$

Returning to the next Yule-Walker equation, 

$$
\operatorname{E} [ Y _ {t} Y _ {t - 2} ] = \operatorname{E} [ \phi_ {1} Y _ {t - 1} Y _ {t - 2} ] + \operatorname{E} [ \theta_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 1} Y _ {t - 2} ] + \operatorname{E} [ \varepsilon_ {t} Y _ {t - 2} ]
$$

and so $\gamma _ { 2 } = \phi _ { 1 } \gamma _ { 1 }$ , and, dividing both sized by γ<sub>0</sub>, $\rho _ { 2 } = \phi _ { 1 } \rho _ { 1 }$ . Higher order autocovariances and autocorrelation follow $\gamma _ { s } = \phi _ { 1 } \gamma _ { s - 1 }$ and $\rho _ { s } = \phi _ { 1 } \rho _ { s - 1 }$ respectively, and so $\rho _ { s } = \phi _ { 1 } ^ { s - 1 } \rho _ { 1 } , s \geq 2$ 

## 4.A.2 Backward Substitution

Backward substitution is a direct but tedious method to derive the ACF and long-run variance. 

## 4.A.2.1 AR(1)

The AR(1) process, 

$$
Y _ {t} = \phi_ {1} Y _ {t - 1} + \varepsilon_ {t}
$$

is stationary if $| \phi _ { 1 } | < 1$ and $\left\{ \varepsilon _ { t } \right\}$ is white noise. To compute the autocovariances and autocorrelations using backward substitution, $Y _ { t } = \phi _ { 1 } Y _ { t - 1 } + \varepsilon _ { t }$ must be transformed into a pure MA process by recursive substitution, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} Y _ {t} = \phi_ {1} Y _ {t - 1} + \varepsilon_ {t} \\ \qquad = \phi_ {1} (\phi_ {1} Y _ {t - 2} + \varepsilon_ {t - 1}) + \varepsilon_ {t} \\ \qquad = \phi_ {1} ^ {2} Y _ {t - 2} + \phi_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 1} + \varepsilon_ {t} \\ \qquad = \phi_ {1} ^ {2} (\phi_ {1} Y _ {t - 3} + \varepsilon_ {t - 2}) + \phi_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 1} + \varepsilon_ {t} \\ \qquad = \phi_ {1} ^ {3} Y _ {t - 3} + \phi_ {1} ^ {2} \varepsilon_ {t - 2} + \phi_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 1} + \varepsilon_ {t} \\ \qquad = \varepsilon_ {t} + \phi_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 1} + \phi_ {1} ^ {2} \varepsilon_ {t - 2} + \phi_ {1} ^ {3} \varepsilon_ {t - 3} + \ldots \\ Y _ {t} = \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {\infty} \phi_ {1} ^ {i} \varepsilon_ {t - i}. \end{array}\tag{4.132}
$$

The variance is the expectation of the square, 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\gamma_ {0} = \mathrm{V} [ Y _ {t} ] = \mathrm{E} [ Y _ {t} ^ {2} ]} \\ & {\qquad = \mathrm{E} [ (\sum_ {i = 0} ^ {\infty} \phi_ {1} ^ {i} \varepsilon_ {t - i}) ^ {2} ]} \\ & {\qquad = \mathrm{E} [ (\varepsilon_ {t} + \phi_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 1} + \phi_ {1} ^ {2} \varepsilon_ {t - 2} + \phi_ {1} ^ {3} \varepsilon_ {t - 3} + \dots) ^ {2} ]} \\ & {\qquad = \mathrm{E} [ \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {\infty} \phi_ {1} ^ {2 i} \varepsilon_ {t - i} ^ {2} + \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {\infty} \sum_ {j = 0, i \neq j} ^ {\infty} \phi_ {1} ^ {i} \phi_ {1} ^ {j} \varepsilon_ {t - i} \varepsilon_ {t - j} ]} \\ & {\qquad = \mathrm{E} [ \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {\infty} \phi_ {1} ^ {2 i} \varepsilon_ {t - i} ^ {2} ] + \mathrm{E} [ \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {\infty} \sum_ {j = 0, i \neq j} ^ {\infty} \phi_ {1} ^ {i} \phi_ {1} ^ {j} \varepsilon_ {t - i} \varepsilon_ {t - j} ]} \\ & {\qquad = \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {\infty} \phi_ {1} ^ {2 i} \mathrm{E} [ \varepsilon_ {t - i} ^ {2} ] + \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {\infty} \sum_ {j = 0, i \neq j} ^ {\infty} \phi_ {1} ^ {i} \phi_ {1} ^ {j} \mathrm{E} [ \varepsilon_ {t - i} \varepsilon_ {t - j} ]} \\ & {\qquad = \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {\infty} \phi_ {1} ^ {2 i} \sigma^ {2} + \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {\infty} \sum_ {j = 0, i \neq j} ^ {\infty} \phi_ {1} ^ {i} \phi_ {1} ^ {j} 0} \\ & {\qquad = \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {\infty} \phi_ {1} ^ {2 i} \sigma^ {2}} \\ & {\qquad = \frac {\sigma^ {2}}{1 - \phi_ {1} ^ {2 i}}} \end{array}\tag{4.133}
$$

The difficult step in the derivation is splitting up the $\varepsilon _ { t - i }$ into those that are matched to their own lag $( \varepsilon _ { t - i } ^ { 2 } )$ to those which are not $( \varepsilon _ { t - i } \varepsilon _ { t - j } , i \neq j )$ . The remainder of the derivation follows from the assumption that $\left\{ \varepsilon _ { t } \right\}$ is a white noise process, and so $\operatorname { E } [ \varepsilon _ { t - i } ^ { 2 } ] = \sigma ^ { 2 }$ and $\operatorname { E } [ \pmb { \varepsilon } _ { t - i } \pmb { \varepsilon } _ { t - j } ] = 0 , i \neq j$ Finally, the identity that $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } \sum _ { i = 0 } ^ { n } \phi _ { 1 } ^ { 2 i } = \operatorname* { l i m } _ { n \to \infty } \sum _ { i = 0 } ^ { n } \left( \phi _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } \right) ^ { i } = \frac { 1 } { 1 - \phi _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } } } \end{array}$ for $| \phi _ { 1 } | < 1$ was used to simplify the expression.The 1st autocovariance can be computed using the same steps on the $\mathbf { M A } ( \infty )$ representation, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \gamma_ {1} = \operatorname{E} [ Y _ {t} Y _ {t - 1} ] \\ = \operatorname{E} [ \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {\infty} \phi_ {1} ^ {i} \varepsilon_ {t - i} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {\infty} \phi_ {1} ^ {i - 1} \varepsilon_ {t - i} ] \\ = \operatorname{E} [ (\varepsilon_ {t} + \phi_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 1} + \phi_ {1} ^ {2} \varepsilon_ {t - 2} + \phi_ {1} ^ {3} \varepsilon_ {t - 3} + \dots) (\varepsilon_ {t - 1} + \phi_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 2} + \phi_ {1} ^ {2} \varepsilon_ {t - 3} + \phi_ {1} ^ {3} \varepsilon_ {t - 4} + \dots) ] \\ = \operatorname{E} [ \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {\infty} \phi_ {1} ^ {2 i + 1} \varepsilon_ {t - 1 - i} ^ {2} + \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {\infty} \sum_ {j = 1, i \neq j} ^ {\infty} \phi_ {1} ^ {i} \phi_ {1} ^ {j - 1} \varepsilon_ {t - i} \varepsilon_ {t - j} ] \\ = \operatorname{E} [ \phi_ {1} \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {\infty} \phi_ {1} ^ {2 i} \varepsilon_ {t - 1 - i} ^ {2} ] + \operatorname{E} [ \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {\infty} \sum_ {j = 1, i \neq j} ^ {\infty} \phi_ {1} ^ {i} \phi_ {1} ^ {j - 1} \varepsilon_ {t - i} \varepsilon_ {t - j} ] \\ = \phi_ {1} \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {\infty} \phi_ {1} ^ {2 i} \operatorname{E} [ \varepsilon_ {t - 1 - i} ^ {2} ] + \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {\infty} \sum_ {j = 1, i \neq j} ^ {\infty} \phi_ {1} ^ {i} \phi_ {1} ^ {j - 1} \operatorname{E} [ \varepsilon_ {t - i} \varepsilon_ {t - j} ] \\ = \phi_ {1} \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {\infty} \phi_ {1} ^ {2 i} \sigma^ {2} + \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {\infty} \sum_ {j = 1, i \neq j} ^ {\infty} \phi_ {1} ^ {i} \phi_ {1} ^ {j - 1} 0 \\ = \phi_ {1} \left(\sum_ {i = 0} ^ {\infty} \phi_ {1} ^ {2 i} \sigma^ {2}\right) \\ = \phi_ {1} \frac {\sigma^ {2}}{1 - \phi_ {1} ^ {2}} \\ = \phi_ {1} \gamma_ {0} \end{array}\tag{4.134}
$$

and the $\mathrm { s } ^ { \mathrm { t h } }$ autocovariance can be similarly determined. 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \gamma_ {s} = \mathrm{E} [ Y _ {t} Y _ {t - s} ] \\ = \mathrm{E} [ \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {\infty} \phi_ {1} ^ {i} \varepsilon_ {t - i} \sum_ {i = s} ^ {\infty} \phi_ {1} ^ {i - s} \varepsilon_ {t - i} ] \\ = \mathrm{E} [ \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {\infty} \phi_ {1} ^ {2 i + s} \varepsilon_ {t - s - i} ^ {2} + \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {\infty} \sum_ {j = s, i \neq j} ^ {\infty} \phi_ {1} ^ {i} \phi_ {1} ^ {j - s} \varepsilon_ {t - i} \varepsilon_ {t - j} ] \\ = \mathrm{E} [ \phi_ {1} ^ {s} \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {\infty} \phi_ {1} ^ {2 i} \varepsilon_ {t - s - i} ^ {2} ] + \mathrm{E} [ \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {\infty} \sum_ {j = s, i \neq j} ^ {\infty} \phi_ {1} ^ {i} \phi_ {1} ^ {j - s} \varepsilon_ {t - i} \varepsilon_ {t - j} ] \\ = \phi_ {1} ^ {s} \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {\infty} \phi_ {1} ^ {2 i} \sigma^ {2} + \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {\infty} \sum_ {j = s, i \neq j} ^ {\infty} \phi_ {1} ^ {i} \phi_ {1} ^ {j - s} 0 \end{array}\tag{4.135}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{l} {= \phi_ {1} ^ {s} \left(\sum_ {i = 0} ^ {\infty} \phi_ {1} ^ {2 i} \sigma^ {2}\right)} \\ {= \phi_ {1} ^ {s} \gamma_ {0}} \end{array}
$$

Finally, the autocorrelations can be computed from rations of autocovariances, $\rho _ { 1 } = \gamma _ { 1 } / \gamma _ { 0 } = \phi _ { 1 }$ and $\rho _ { s } = \gamma _ { s } / \gamma _ { 0 } = \phi _ { 1 } ^ { s }$ 

## 4.A.2.2 MA(1)

The MA(1) model is the simplest non-degenerate time-series model considered in this course, 

$$
Y _ {t} = \theta_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 1} + \varepsilon_ {t}
$$

and the derivation of its autocorrelation function is trivial since there no backward substitution is required. The variance is 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \gamma_ {0} = \mathrm{V} [ Y _ {t} ] = \mathrm{E} [ Y _ {t} ^ {2} ] \\ \quad = \mathrm{E} [ (\theta_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 1} + \varepsilon_ {t}) ^ {2} ] \\ \quad = \mathrm{E} [ \theta_ {1} ^ {2} \varepsilon_ {t - 1} ^ {2} + 2 \theta_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t} \varepsilon_ {t - 1} + \varepsilon_ {t} ^ {2} ] \\ \quad = \mathrm{E} [ \theta_ {1} ^ {2} \varepsilon_ {t - 1} ^ {2} ] + \mathrm{E} [ 2 \theta_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t} \varepsilon_ {t - 1} ] + \mathrm{E} [ \varepsilon_ {t} ^ {2} ] \\ \quad = \theta_ {1} ^ {2} \sigma^ {2} + 0 + \sigma^ {2} \\ \quad = \sigma^ {2} (1 + \theta_ {1} ^ {2}) \end{array}\tag{4.136}
$$

and the 1st autocovariance is 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \gamma_ {1} = \mathrm{E} [ Y _ {t} Y _ {t - 1} ] \\ = \mathrm{E} [ (\theta_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 1} + \varepsilon_ {t}) (\theta_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 2} + \varepsilon_ {t - 1}) ] \\ = \mathrm{E} [ \theta_ {1} ^ {2} \varepsilon_ {t - 1} \varepsilon_ {t - 2} + \theta_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 1} ^ {2} + \theta_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t} \varepsilon_ {t - 2} + \varepsilon_ {t} \varepsilon_ {t - 1} ] \\ = \mathrm{E} [ \theta_ {1} ^ {2} \varepsilon_ {t - 1} \varepsilon_ {t - 2} ] + \mathrm{E} [ \theta_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 1} ^ {2} ] + \mathrm{E} [ \theta_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t} \varepsilon_ {t - 2} ] + \mathrm{E} [ \varepsilon_ {t} \varepsilon_ {t - 1} ] \\ = 0 + \theta_ {1} \sigma^ {2} + 0 + 0 \\ = \theta_ {1} \sigma^ {2} \end{array}\tag{4.137}
$$

The $2 ^ { \mathrm { n d } }$ (and higher) autocovariance is 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \gamma_ {2} = \mathrm{E} [ Y _ {t} Y _ {t - 2} ] \\ \quad = \mathrm{E} [ (\theta_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 1} + \varepsilon_ {t}) (\theta_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 3} + \varepsilon_ {t - 2}) ] \\ \quad = \mathrm{E} [ \theta_ {1} ^ {2} \varepsilon_ {t - 1} \varepsilon_ {t - 3} + \theta_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 1} \varepsilon_ {t - 2} + \theta_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t} \varepsilon_ {t - 3} + \varepsilon_ {t} \varepsilon_ {t - 2} ] \\ \quad = \mathrm{E} [ \theta_ {1} ^ {2} \varepsilon_ {t - 1} \varepsilon_ {t - 3} ] + \mathrm{E} [ \theta_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 1} \varepsilon_ {t - 2} ] + \mathrm{E} [ \theta_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t} \varepsilon_ {t - 3} ] + \mathrm{E} [ \varepsilon_ {t} \varepsilon_ {t - 2} ] \\ \quad = 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 \\ \quad = 0 \end{array}\tag{4.138}
$$

and the autocorrelations are $\rho _ { 1 } = \theta _ { 1 } / ( 1 + \theta _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } ) , \rho _ { s } = 0 , s \geq 2 .$ 

## 4.A.2.3 ARMA(1,1)

An ARMA(1,1) process, 

$$
Y _ {t} = \phi_ {1} Y _ {t - 1} + \theta_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 1} + \varepsilon_ {t}
$$

is stationary if $| \phi _ { 1 } | < 1$ and $\left\{ \varepsilon _ { t } \right\}$ is white noise. The derivation of the variance and autocovariances is more tedious than for the AR(1) process. It should be noted that derivation is longer and more complex than solving the Yule-Walker equations.Begin by computing the MA( ) representation,

\begin{array}{l} Y _ {t} = \phi_ {1} Y _ {t - 1} + \theta_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 1} + \varepsilon_ {t} \\ Y _ {t} = \phi_ {1} (\phi_ {1} Y _ {t - 2} + \theta_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 2} + \varepsilon_ {t - 1}) + \theta_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 1} + \varepsilon_ {t} \\ Y _ {t} = \phi_ {1} ^ {2} Y _ {t - 2} + \phi_ {1} \theta_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 2} + \phi_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 1} + \theta_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 1} + \varepsilon_ {t} \\ Y _ {t} = \phi_ {1} ^ {2} (\phi_ {1} Y _ {t - 3} + \theta_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 3} + \varepsilon_ {t - 2}) + \phi_ {1} \theta_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 2} + (\phi_ {1} + \theta_ {1}) \varepsilon_ {t - 1} + \varepsilon_ {t} \\ Y _ {t} = \phi_ {1} ^ {3} Y _ {t - 3} + \phi_ {1} ^ {2} \theta_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 3} + \phi_ {1} ^ {2} \varepsilon_ {t - 2} + \phi_ {1} \theta_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 2} + (\phi_ {1} + \theta_ {1}) \varepsilon_ {t - 1} + \varepsilon_ {t} \\ Y _ {t} = \phi_ {1} ^ {3} (\phi_ {1} Y _ {t - 4} + \theta_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 4} + \\ Y _ {t} = \phi_ {1} ^ {4} Y _ {t - 4} + \phi_ {1} ^ {3} \theta_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 4} + \phi_ {1} ^ {3} \varepsilon_ {t - 3} + \phi_ {1} ^ {2} \theta_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 3} + \phi_ {1} (\phi_ {1} + \theta_ {1}) \varepsilon_ {t - 2} + (\phi_ {1} + \theta_ {1}) \varepsilon_ {t - 1} + \varepsilon_ {t} \\ Y _ {t}   =   \phi_ {1} ^ {4} Y _ {t - 4} + \phi_ {1} ^ {3} \theta_ {1} \varepsilon_ {t - 4} + \phi_ {1} ^ {2} (\phi_ {1} + \theta_ {1}) \varepsilon_ {t - 3} + \phi_ {1} (\phi_ {1} + \theta_ {1}) \varepsilon_ {t - 2} + (\phi_ {1} + \theta_ {1}) \varepsilon_ {t - 1} + \varepsilon_ {t} \\ Y _ {t} = \varepsilon_ {t} + (\phi_ {1} + \theta_ {1}) \varepsilon_ {t - 1} + \phi_ {1} (\phi_ {1} + \theta_ {1}) \varepsilon_ {t - 2} + \phi_ {1} ^ {2} (\phi_ {1} + \theta_ {1}) \varepsilon_ {t - 3} |\tag{4.139}
$$

The primary issue is that the backward substitution form, unlike in the AR(1) case, is not completely symmetric. Specifically, $\varepsilon _ { t }$ has a different weight than the other shocks and does not follow the same pattern. 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \gamma_ {0} = \mathrm{V} [ Y _ {t} ] = \mathrm{E} [ Y _ {t} ^ {2} ] \\ = \mathrm{E} \left[ \left(\varepsilon_ {t} + \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {\infty} \phi_ {1} ^ {i} (\phi_ {1} + \theta_ {1}) \varepsilon_ {t - 1 - i}\right) ^ {2} \right] \\ = \mathrm{E} \left[ \left(\varepsilon_ {t} + (\phi_ {1} + \theta_ {1}) \varepsilon_ {t - 1} + \phi_ {1} (\phi_ {1} + \theta_ {1}) \varepsilon_ {t - 2} + \phi_ {1} ^ {2} (\phi_ {1} + \theta_ {1}) \varepsilon_ {t - 3} + \dots\right) ^ {2} \right] \\ = \mathrm{E} \left[ \varepsilon_ {t} ^ {2} + 2 \varepsilon_ {t} \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {\infty} \phi_ {1} ^ {i} (\phi_ {1} + \theta_ {1}) \varepsilon_ {t - 1 - i} + \left(\sum_ {i = 0} ^ {\infty} \phi_ {1} ^ {i} (\phi_ {1} + \theta_ {1}) \varepsilon_ {t - 1 - i}\right) ^ {2} \right] \\ = \mathrm{E} [ \varepsilon_ {t} ^ {2} ] + \mathrm{E} \left[ 2 \varepsilon_ {t} \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {\infty} \phi_ {1} ^ {i} (\phi_ {1} + \theta_ {1}) \varepsilon_ {t - 1 - i} \right] + \mathrm{E} \left[ \left(\sum_ {i = 0} ^ {\infty} \phi_ {1} ^ {i} (\phi_ {1} + \theta_ {1}) \varepsilon_ {t - 1 - i}\right) ^ {2} \right] \\ = \sigma^ {2} + 0 + \mathrm{E} \left[ \left(\sum_ {i = 0} ^ {\infty} \phi_ {1} ^ {i} (\phi_ {1} + \theta_ {1}) \varepsilon_ {t - 1 - i}\right) ^ {2} \right] \\ = \sigma^ {2} + \mathrm{E} \left[ \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {\infty} \phi_ {1} ^ {2 i} (\phi_ {1} + \theta_ {1}) ^ {2} \varepsilon_ {t - 1 - i} ^ {2} + \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {\infty} \sum_ {j = 0, j \neq i} ^ {\infty} \phi_ {1} ^ {i} \phi_ {1} ^ {j} (\phi_ {1} + \theta_ {1}) ^ {2} \varepsilon_ {t - 1 - i} \varepsilon_ {t - 1 - j} \right] \end{array}\tag{4.140}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{l} = \sigma^ {2} + \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {\infty} \phi_ {1} ^ {2 i} (\phi_ {1} + \theta_ {1}) ^ {2} \mathrm{E} [ \varepsilon_ {t - 1 - i} ^ {2} ] + \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {\infty} \sum_ {j = 0, j \neq i} ^ {\infty} \phi_ {1} ^ {i} \phi_ {1} ^ {j} (\phi_ {1} + \theta_ {1}) ^ {2} \mathrm{E} [ \varepsilon_ {t - 1 - i} \varepsilon_ {t - 1 - j} ] \\ = \sigma^ {2} + \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {\infty} \phi_ {1} ^ {2 i} (\phi_ {1} + \theta_ {1}) ^ {2} \sigma^ {2} + \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {\infty} \sum_ {j = 0, j \neq i} ^ {\infty} \phi_ {1} ^ {i} \phi_ {1} ^ {j} (\phi_ {1} + \theta_ {1}) ^ {2} 0 \\ = \sigma^ {2} + \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {\infty} \phi_ {1} ^ {2 i} (\phi_ {1} + \theta_ {1}) ^ {2} \sigma^ {2} \\ = \sigma^ {2} + \frac {(\phi_ {1} + \theta_ {1}) ^ {2} \sigma^ {2}}{1 - \phi_ {1} ^ {2}} \\ = \sigma^ {2} \frac {1 - \phi_ {1} ^ {2} + (\phi_ {1} + \theta_ {1}) ^ {2}}{1 - \phi_ {1} ^ {2}} \\ = \sigma^ {2} \frac {1 + \theta_ {1} ^ {2} + 2 \phi_ {1} \theta_ {1}}{1 - \phi_ {1} ^ {2}} \end{array}
$$

The difficult step in this derivations is in aligning the $\varepsilon _ { t - i }$ since $\left\{ \varepsilon _ { t } \right\}$ is a white noise process. The autocovariance derivation is reasonably involved (and presented in full detail). 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \gamma_ {1} = \mathrm{E} \left[ Y _ {t} Y _ {t - 1} \right] \\ = \mathrm{E} \left[ \left(\varepsilon_ {t} + \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {\infty} \phi_ {1} ^ {i} (\phi_ {1} + \theta_ {1}) \varepsilon_ {t - 1 - i}\right) \left(\varepsilon_ {t - 1} + \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {\infty} \phi_ {1} ^ {i} (\phi_ {1} + \theta_ {1}) \varepsilon_ {t - 2 - i}\right) \right] \\ = \mathrm{E} \left[ \left(\varepsilon_ {t} + (\phi_ {1} + \theta_ {1}) \varepsilon_ {t - 1} + \phi_ {1} (\phi_ {1} + \theta_ {1}) \varepsilon_ {t - 2} + \phi_ {1} ^ {2} (\phi_ {1} + \theta_ {1}) \varepsilon_ {t - 3} + \dots\right) \times \right. \\ \left. \left(\varepsilon_ {t - 1} + (\phi_ {1} + \theta_ {1}) \varepsilon_ {t - 2} + \phi_ {1} (\phi_ {1} + \theta_ {1}) \varepsilon_ {t - 3} + \phi_ {1} ^ {2} (\phi_ {1} + \theta_ {1}) \varepsilon_ {t - 4} + \dots\right) \right] \\ = \mathrm{E} \left[ \varepsilon_ {t} \varepsilon_ {t - 1} + \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {\infty} \phi_ {1} ^ {i} (\phi_ {1} + \theta_ {1})
